News.title: Groom-to-be, 24, found dead in rubble after 7.4-magnitude earthquake rocks Colombia just 2 days before his wedding
News.content:
QUAKE TRAGEDY Groom-to-be, 24, found dead in rubble after 7.4-magnitude earthquake rocks Colombia just 2 days before his wedding

THE body of a groom-to-be who was just two days away from his wedding has been found in the rubble of a collapsed hotel in Colombia.

Juan Felipe Giraldo, 24, was due to marry the mother of his child, Natalia Patiño, on August 16 when he went missing in the city of Pereira.



After news of his disappearance emerged, Juan’s father, Hernán Giraldo, travelled to Pereira and joined rescue teams searching day and night for his son.

Juan had reportedly sent his fiancée a video shortly before the disaster, which helped rescuers pinpoint his location after the earthquake caused the hotel to collapse.



Before his son’s body was discovered, Hernán said in a heartbreaking video: “There is life, there are small signs of life, and if there is life there is hope.

“Son, I love you. On Sunday you are going to be getting married, and if not on Sunday, it will be in eight, 15 days, but you will be there, son.”



But the family’s worst fears were realised when Juan was eventually found dead.

“Forever and always my heart, you were the most complete love I ever had. I love you forever,” his grieving fiancée wrote on Instagram.



The couple had a two-year-old son and lived together in Colombia‘s capital, Bogotá.

Juan had travelled to Pereira on a work trip just hours before the deadly quake struck, and ended up staying at the doomed Hotel Dibeni in the city centre.

This comes after a triplet had her life ripped apart after losing both of her sisters and her parents in Colombia’s devastating 7.4-magnitude earthquake.

Ana María Saavedra, 23, was pulled alive from the rubble of her destroyed four-storey home in Cali, the worst-hit city.

She survived after taking shelter beneath a sturdy wooden table as the building came crashing down around her.



But her parents, Jairo Hernán Saavedra, 63, and Victoria Caicedo, 61, were tragically found dead in each other’s arms.

Her sister Sofía was also killed after becoming trapped beneath a collapsed staircase.

And the body of Ana María’s third triplet, Isabella, was recovered late on Thursday night.

The earthquake struck at a depth of around 64 miles in Chocó province and was felt across a vast area of western Colombia.

Tremors were felt hundreds of miles away in Venezuela’s capital, Caracas, as well as across parts of Ecuador and Panama.



Officials said 294 people had been confirmed dead and 3,935 injured, according to a Saturday report from Colombia’s National Unit for Disaster Risk Management (UNGRD).

Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella has deployed 1,000 members of the security forces to Cali following reports of looting.

The disaster is an early test for the president, who was inaugurated just days ago on August 7.

On Tuesday, he flew to Pereira with his wife, First Lady Ana Lucía Pineda, to inspect one of the worst-hit areas.

“My commitment is to each and every one of the affected families,” he wrote on X.



“We remain on the ground, working for our people.”

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said America “stands ready to support” Colombia.

The US Department of State described the disaster as “devastating” and pledged £11.5million to provide emergency shelter and supplies.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The EU is also providing funding and supporting rescue operations, foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said.

The Colombian government has meanwhile announced an immediate emergency rent subsidy for people who have lost their homes.

News.title: M56 shut near Manchester Airport after major crash as car on fire and emergency crews swarm scene
News.content:
CRASH CHAOS M56 shut near Manchester Airport after major crash as car on fire and emergency crews swarm scene

THE M56 has been shut near a major airport following a multi-vehicle crash causing one car to catch fire.

Emergency services have rushed to the M56 in Cheshire near Manchester Airport and closed the road eastbound between J7 Bowden Interchange and J6 Hale Four Seasons Interchange.

The road was shut early this morning as the crash caused one car to overturn and another to become engulfed in flames.

Greater Manchester Police, Greater Manchester Fire and Rescue, and paramedics from North West Ambulance Service have raced to the scene.





Due to the severity of the crash, the road surface and barriers need to be inspected before other vehicles can use the motorway.

There is currently two miles of congestion with those heading to Manchester Airport advised to allow extra time for their journey.

A national highways spokesperson said: “The M56 eastbound between J7 and J6 near Manchester Airport is being closed following a two-car collision.

“One of the cars has overturned. The other car has caught fire.

“The collision has resulted in infrastructure damage.

“National Highways contractors are being despatched to scene to inspect the nearside barrier and road surface as well as support in implementing the closure of the motorway.

“Current delays of 20 mins on approach and two miles of congestion.”

News.title: Cops launch urgent hunt for missing teenage sisters, 14 & 15, who vanished from UK city three days ago
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

FIND THEM Cops launch urgent hunt for missing teenage sisters, 14 & 15, who vanished from UK city three days ago

COPS have launched an urgent hunt for two teenage sisters who vanished from a UK city.

Concerns are growing for Summer, 14, and Skye, 15, who vanished from Truro, Cornwall, three days ago.



The sisters were reported missing from the cathedral city on Friday, sparking an urgent police hunt.

They are believed to have travelled to nearby areas Redruth, Penryn or Falmouth, according to Devon and Cornwall Police.



The force has urged anyone with more information on their disappearance to come forward.

Issuing a statement, it said: “We are becoming increasingly concerned for the welfare of sisters Summer, 14, and Skye, 15, from West Cornwall.



“The girls were last seen in Truro and were reported missing on Friday 14 August.

“Summer and Skye are believed to be in the Redruth, Penryn or Falmouth areas.

“If you have seen either of them or have any information that may help us locate them, please contact police quoting reference 399 of 14/08/26.

“You can report information by calling 101, or 999 in an emergency.”

News.title: Britain set for SIXTH heatwave as Met Office says record-breaking summer will continue after gloomy week of rain
News.content:
A SIXTH heatwave could grip Britain next month as record-breaking temperatures may continue into Autumn.

The Met Office has warned of a potential heatwave in September according to its long-range weather forecast.



Following showers and long spells of rain this week, the mercury could climb high as we enter the autumn period due to high pressure – particularly in the south.

However, it’s too early to predict just how severe a sixth potential heatwave could be.



The forecaster said: “As we move into the start of meteorological autumn, signals for the prevailing weather patterns affecting the UK are weak, thus something close to the climatological norm is most likely.

“This means a broad northwest-southeast split in conditions, with the high pressure becoming centred close to the south of the UK and more changeable conditions developing towards the north and northwest.

“Meanwhile, drier, more settled weather is slightly more likely towards the south and east. Temperatures are likely to be above average overall.

“There is a chance that late season hot spells or heatwaves develop, especially in the south.”



It comes after an increased amount of rain is expected to fall this week, making its way across the country, bringing breezier conditions.

From Monday onwards, the north will see cloud and outbreaks of heavy showers, which will gradually move southward.

The Met Office added: “Temperatures are more likely to be above normal than below overall, though the possibility of widespread or exceptional heat is lower than in recent weeks.”

There is predicted to be widespread rain on Thursday after nearly three-quarters of England and the entirety of Wales is facing drought.

In response to the dry conditions, over 27million Brits currently face hosepipe ban restrictions.



These have been enforced by nine water companies to prevent unnecessary water use.

Last week, the UK saw temperatures reach highs of 38C in the country’s fifth heatwave of the year last week.

A rare amber alert for heat was issued across the nation, and two trains derailed within 24 hours.

The first incident occurred on Thursday in Lewes, East Sussex with two seriously injured, and the second happened in Wickford, Essex.

Network Rail bosses have suggested the heat may have been to blame and investigations are under way.

News.title: Burnham’s political sweeties are just more meaningless policies… It’s time he stopped tinkering and faced real problem
News.content:
TOO often I find myself thinking back to Rachel Reeves’ first Budget and wondering whether it’s within the grasp of man to drink 550 pints of lager.

That is not, in fact, the exact amount of booze needed to vaporise every last brain cell and wipe her calamitous tax hikes from memory.



It was certainly a day to forget as the Chancellor did her best Eeyore impression over the parlous state of public finances.

But she did give Labour MPs something to celebrate when announcing a cut to the duty on draught beer.



“Which means a penny off a pint in the pub!” she roared, to much guffawing from the benches behind her.

I too would have cheered had we all time-travelled back to the 1960s when a pint was 8p.

But these days a Stella in most establishments will set you back at least £5.50, and so you would have to sink at least 550 cold ones before the next one paid for itself.

(I reckon I could handle about 12 in one session before it’s Goodnight Vienna.)

Politicians have this extraordinary knack of hamming up virtually meaningless policies as some great triumph deserving of public gratitude.

And so it has become with Andy Burnham’s recent bag of goodies designed to give people “breathing room” with the cost of living.



He shaved VAT from energy bills (a great Brexit benefit) to save families £45 a year.

Bus fares have been capped at £2 rather than £3, in a return to the policy first launched under the Tories.

And he has promised to end “subscription traps” for numpties who signed up for free trials and are then shocked when money comes out of their account the next month.

This could save a whole £14, according to Treasury boffins.

These off-the-shelf ideas that are flashy yet inexpensive have given the PM something to parade to voters in his first few weeks.



(If he is still in the market, may I suggest freezing the BBC licence fee — or voiding it altogether — and telling them to make up the losses by cutting eye-watering staff costs.)

While the numbers may be small, the politics are not insignificant for a man eager to ingratiate himself to a sceptical electorate.

But let’s not pretend it’s anything other than peanuts.



And let’s also not pretend that this tinkering is something happening only under Burnham. It isn’t.

All recent governments have been guilty of reaching for eye-catching baubles while ignoring the deep structural changes Britain is crying out for.

Which brings me to the October 28 Budget.

Recent Budgets have been tantamount to fiddling while Rome burns.

If our economy were a clockface, then politicians spend their time arguing whether we should nudge the little hand by a few minutes back and forth.



Spend a few billion here, tax a few billion there.

If the Office for Budget Responsibility is satisfied that the numbers stack up, then it’s job done.

Except that is no way to run a country.

We spend, we tax, and all the while, growth is on the floor and debt is through the roof.

The UK national debt currently stands at £3trillion. That’s 12 zeros, by the way.



This galactic tab means each year to pay off the interest alone on that debt is more than £100billion — more than we’ll spend on defence and prisons in their entirety.

New Chancellor, John Healey, is a smart chap who appreciates the scale of the task.

But this will also take Labour MPs finally making contact with economic reality, especially around welfare which has become nothing short of a national disgrace.



That Britain will spend £400billion each year by the end of this decade on welfare is so obviously nuts.

And still . . .

Reform is today pledging to cut £50billion from the benefits bill by clamping down on out-of-control sickness claims.

Although we await the detail, these are the sorts of numbers we need to be talking about.

Depressingly, Labour flew out of the traps, decrying such cuts as “fantasy economics”.



But it is them living in Cloud Cuckoo Land if they think current levels are remotely sustainable.

For a generation of MPs bred to hate “austerity” — previously known as spending what you can afford — is there any hope?

Burnham must make his party see sense on debt.

There are many persuasive arguments, including that cutting the crippling interest will actually free up funds currently being burned to spend more on priorities.

Burnham has the political capital and goodwill to be temporarily unpopular, especially if we take him at his word that the next election will be 2029.



He might get a cheer and a headline for all the sweeties he’s been handing out.

But I’ll be raising a glass if he starts cutting spending, rather than adding to it.

LIKE Keir Starmer, Andy Burnham is a genuine football fan.

The Prime Minister has even renewed his Everton season ticket, which makes you wonder if that could be the real reason behind opening a Number 10 North.

Already he has raised hopes by suggesting he could lift the long-standing ban on drinking in the stands at games.



So I wonder if Mr Burnham could go one step further and end the hated 3pm blackout. The 1960s-era law that bans football matches being shown on telly between 2.45pm and 5.15pm on Saturdays is from another time.

Originally intended to force people to attend matches in person, it is now just by-passed by fans crowding round illegal livestreams at home.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Attending games in person is becoming increasingly difficult and expensive for supporters at the hands of greedy fat cats. And just think of what a boon it would be for hard-up pubs if Saturday games drove people to the boozer.

Landlords I speak to say the World Cup was a merciful golden period in an otherwise tough market. Ending the bonkers blackout would be a tap-in, PM.

News.title: Missing fisherman, 31, rescued ALIVE after spending 15 days trapped 300ft down pitch-black underwater cave
News.content:
A FISHERMAN has been rescued after a harrowing 15-days trapped 300ft down a water-filled sinkhole.

Erasto Crisanto Valdez ,31, vanished while fishing with his father in a cenote in San Francisco La Paz, Mexico, on July 23.



After over two weeks missing, rescuers presumed the man as dead and were “prepared to find his body”.

By some miracle he was found alive – reportedly trapped in a cave with an air pocket more than 328ft below the surface.



He was discovered on Thursday by a international team of explorers from Mexico, Germany, the US and the Dominican Republic after facing weeks of cold and humidity in the dark cave.

Mexican explorer Carlos Jiménez described the discovery as a miracle saying “god had other plans” for the lucky man.



In an interview with NMás, Erasto said: “Thank you god for giving me another opportunity at life and letting me see my kids and family again.

“It was a miracle – an unbelievable miracle”



Following his initial disappearance, a search operation began immediately, but searches in the water yielded no results.

Six days into the desperate search rescuers discovered found the harpoon Erasto.

The depth of the cenote and the difficult conditions at the site made it challenging to locate Erasto.



A cenote is a deep natural well or sinkhole formed by the collapse of surface limestone, exposing groundwater beneath.

Erasto was then brought to the surface on a stretcher.

He was found to be suffering from severe dehydration and malnutrition after spending more than two weeks without access to food,

He was rushed to hospital for treatment in his hometown of Uxpanapa.

It comes as five people were saved from a flooded cave in Laos after they became trapped.



Thai rescuers successfully pulled five of the seven villagers from the tiny after torrential rain triggered landslides that sealed the entrance in May.

The villagers ventured into the remote cave in Xaysomboun province in May reportedly hunting for wildlife and searching for gold.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Sadly two men were never found as the active search was called off when rescue teams deemed it too dangerous.

The rescue was led by the same team who saved the Thai football team who became trapped in the Tham Luang Nang Non cave system in 2018.

News.title: Iran military chief threatens to ‘break Trump’s legs’ after US leader vowed to make Strait of Hormuz American territory
News.content:
ONE of Iran’s top military chiefs has threatened to break Donald Trump’s legs after the US President vowed to make the Strait of Hormuz American territory.

Responding to Trump’s incendiary remarks, Major General Amir Hatami said joking about such a move was a “major mistake” because Iran had defenders who would “break your legs”.



He also claimed US forces had been “effectively driven out” of the region and would no longer be permitted to enter the fiercely contested Strait of Hormuz.

Iranian officials had previously told the White House to “accept the reality of defeat” after Tehran declared it would not resume talks with Washington.



The comments came after Trump confidently declared that the crucial gateway to the Gulf would one day become “a territory of the United States”.

Trump said: “After we finish defeating Iran, which is being very badly defeated – pretty soon, I’ll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States.”



“Essentially, that’s what it is. We have the blockade.

“No ships get through unless we want them to.”



Before the US launched strikes on Iran earlier this year, the Strait of Hormuz was one of the world’s most crucial maritime routes for oil tankers.

But since the outbreak of war, passage through the strait has become increasingly difficult and, at times, has been completely halted.

The disruption has sent shockwaves through global markets, with oil prices soaring amid fears over supplies.

With no imminent peace deal in sight, Hatami also announced a $30,000 bounty for any US service member who is captured or killed.

“Given the large volume of requests to participate in the financial jihad, a plan was prepared according to which, for every person who kills or captures and hands over an American aggressor force, the Islamic Republic of Iran Army, with the support of the loved ones participating in the financial jihad and under its own guarantee, will receive a gift equivalent to $30,000 or 5 billion Tomans,” Hatami said.



“The weapon of any person who succeeds in killing an American aggressor will be purchased at double the price and will receive a new weapon.

“The individual’s weapon will also be kept in a planned museum.”

The Iranian military chief also issued a stark warning to US forces and bases across the Middle East.



“Everyone should know that in no way can the American bases return to their previous status, and Iran will never allow centers to be established in our neighborhood that aim to threaten Islamic Iran,” he said.

“The only way is for the Americans to leave the region. They have been effectively expelled and are no longer permitted to enter the Persian Gulf, the Sea of Oman, and the Strait of Hormuz.

“We have won on this path and are consolidating our victory.”

The extraordinary threats come as Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law and envoy, held rare talks with Hamas in a bid to revive the stalled Gaza peace process.

Kushner met with a senior Hamas leader on Sunday as part of a renewed diplomatic push to advance the US-backed ceasefire plan.



He is due to meet Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Monday for talks aimed at salvaging a 15-point roadmap backed by Washington.

The plan requires Hamas to disarm in Gaza while Israel withdraws its forces from the war-torn territory.

At stake is the future of around two million people in Gaza and the reconstruction of the densely populated enclave, which remains largely under Israeli military control more than 10 months after the ceasefire halted major fighting.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

A meeting last year between Kushner, fellow US envoy Steve Witkoff and Hamas leaders in Egypt helped secure the original ceasefire.

But the agreement has since stalled over the key issue of Hamas disarmament.

News.title: Cops launch fresh appeal four years after murder of man, 22, as balaclava-clad gang still terrorising city
News.content:
MURDER RIDDLE Cops launch fresh appeal four years after murder of man, 22, as balaclava-clad gang still terrorising city

COPS have launched a fresh appeal for information four years on from the murder of a man as a balaclava-clad gang continue to terrorise the city.

Sam Rimmer, 22, was fatally shot in August 2022 at Lavrock Bank, Liverpool with ten people previously arrested – but no one has been charged.



It’s the four-year anniversary of when Sam was hit by one of eight bullets fired from an e-bike rider using a Czech-made military grade firearm.

He had been hanging out with friends when he was tragically caught in the crossfire of gangs battling to dominate the firearms and drugs trade.



Detectives believe the four murder suspects are part of a gang that had previously spent hours circling the area on two bikes to “hunt” for targets.

Wearing black masks, they used a type of horn or engine noise to bait the rival group, before firing towards Sam and his friends – some of who were also hit.

The murder weapon has been identified as a Skorpion sub-machine gun – capable of firing multiple shots in a fraction of a second.

But it has never been recovered and cops are unable to hand out justice unless crucial eye witnesses come forward.



Det Ch Insp Steve McGrath told the BBC: “I would still ask [anyone] to come forward and the reason for that really is I can assure you that the people who are involved in Sam’s murder directly – those four individuals on the bike – are still involved in serious criminality in and around the Dingle area as well.”

Five days after Sam’s death, council worker Ashley Dale, 28, was found dead of a gunshot wound in a back garden in the city’s Old Swan area.

And, Olivia Pratt-Korbel, nine, was also shot dead in her own home after Thomas Cashman burst into the property chasing a local criminal.

The deaths of these innocent people are as a result of a new generation of teen gangs in Merseyside using violence to replace the ‘old mafia’, according to a BBC Panorama investigation.

Speaking on the anniversary of Sam’s death, McGrath, added: “Today marks four years since Sam was murdered and I can only imagine how difficult this occasion must be for his family and friends.



“I want to reassure them, and the wider community in Dingle, that we are still just as determined to find the people responsible as we were four years ago.

“As part of our investigation we have made a number of arrests and received a lot of information from the public. We just need the final piece of the puzzle.

“I’d like to take this opportunity to appeal to anyone who holds any information whatsoever to get in touch. It’s not too late.

“We are certain that someone out there knows who is responsible and could end the family’s agonising wait for answers.

“If anyone out there is keeping information to themselves, I ask you to consider what Sam’s family are going through.



“If you haven’t already, it is now time to come forward with that information.”

Pamela Tompsett, North West Regional Manager at the charity Crimestoppers said: “It’s now four years on from Sam’s tragic murder, his family and friends are still waiting for answers and justice.

“It is possible that someone knows who is responsible or holds information that could help investigators but has not yet felt able to speak directly to the police.

“Crimestoppers is completely independent of the police, and anyone contacting us remains 100 per cent anonymous.

“We have no caller ID, we do not trace IP addresses, and we never ask for personal details.



“The reward of up to £20,000 is available for information we exclusively receive that leads to the conviction of those responsible for Sam’s murder.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“If you know something, however small it may seem, please tell us anonymously. Your information could be the missing piece that helps brings answers for Sam’s family and justice for those responsible.”

Anyone with information should contact Merseyside Police social media desk using X or Facebook @MerPolCC. or by calling 101.

News.title: Five teenagers dead and four injured after car drives on wrong side of motorway
News.content:
Five teenage boys have died and four people have been taken to hospital following a two-vehicle crash in County Kildare.

The collision occurred on the M9 Northbound at Junction 3 at about 03:00 local time on Sunday.

GardaÃ­ said the bodies of the five teenage boys, all occupants of one vehicle, have now been removed from the scene and taken to Naas General Hospital where post mortems will take place.

They said the vehicle had been travelling on the wrong side of the carriageway when a head on collision occurred with a second car.

The driver and front passenger, both female and aged in their 30s, of the second car have been removed from the scene to Tallaght University Hospital and both remain in critical condition.

A female rear seat passenger, aged in her 20s, was taken to St. Luke's General Hospital and is in a serious condition.

The third passenger, who is a child, has been removed to Children's Health Ireland at Crumlin and is in a serious condition.

The section of the M9 from Junction 3 to Junction 4 northbound and southbound remains closed with local diversions in place.

Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly described those injured in the crash as "family members" who were "travelling innocently" when they were struck by the car driving on the wrong side of the motorway.

He described it as a "horrific incident" and "irresponsible and dangerous driving".

"What makes this reckless behaviour even more appalling is that in some cases it is being done for social media likes regardless of the potentially devastating impact it might have on innocent people and themselves."

Kelly added that officers "do what they can to stop such vehicles while also taking into consideration all other road users".

"GardaÃ­ are put in a really challenging situation dealing with such incidents."

News.title: Emergency phone alert put domestic abuse victims at risk, campaigners say
News.content:
Most people received the blaring alert at 19:00 BST on Friday - and it came as a surprise given the government had not told people it was coming, as it has done for tests of the system.

The notification, which cautioned against the use of disposable barbecues, naked flames or fireworks, was the biggest use yet of the emergency alert system and Prime Minister Andy Burnham urged the public to take it "seriously".

A Cabinet Office press release, posted to their website at about 18:45 on Friday, was missed by many in the media, which meant there was little warning to the public.

This potentially jeopardised domestic abuse victims trying to hide secret phones they use to seek support and try to escape abusers, some campaigners have said.

Women's Aid, the national charity aiming to end domestic abuse, is calling for more forewarning of alerts wherever possible.

Veronica Oakeshott, the charity's head of external affairs, told BBC News: "Survivors of domestic abuse frequently turn to second phones to help them access lifesaving support or flee from abuse."

It is vital the devices stay hidden, she said, before adding: "We would urge the government to forewarn the public that alerts might be issued, when possible."

It has been reported that senior government figures were discussing whether or not to send the alert hours before, on Friday morning.

The alert came after a spate of wildfires including one that destroyed 19 homes in Stourbridge, West Midlands, on Thursday.

News.title: Murder inquiry after man bitten by dog dies
News.content:
A murder inquiry has begun after the death of a man who was bitten by a dog on a footpath in West Yorkshire.

The 55-year-old was injured in an altercation on a disused railway line off Blacker Lane in Calder Grove, Wakefield, at about 13:30 BST on Saturday. He was taken to hospital in a critical condition but died just after 19:00.

West Yorkshire Police has appealed for two people, one of whom is called Sophie, who stopped to help the injured man to come forward.

A force spokesperson said a 55-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of murder and of being the owner of a dog dangerously out of control in a public place, causing injury. He remains in custody.

Police said a German Shepherd dog believed to have been involved in the incident has been seized by officers.

Det Ch Insp Michael Cox said: "Sadly, a man has died and it is really important that we understand the circumstances of what has taken place.

"We know that two people, one named Sophie, stopped to assist the injured man and direct officers."

He added: "We would urge these two people to come forward to help us with our ongoing inquiries into this tragic incident.

"The initial altercation happened in an area used by walkers and we are urging anyone who has seen or heard any part of the exchange between these two men to please make contact."

News.title: Calls for public inquiry into Jason Arday 'witch hunt'
News.content:
Green Party leader Zack Polanski, and Labour MPs Bell Ribiero-Addy, Clive Lewis and Nadia Whittome are among the politicians to have signed the statement, alongside former England footballer Eni Aluko, National Education Union general secretary Daniel Kebede, and broadcaster Carol Vorderman.

It calls for an "immediate public inquiry into how to ensure a responsible press".

Arday, 41, was found dead at an address in Battersea, south London, on Friday. He had resigned as a Cambridge professor of sociology of education on 5 August after allegations of plagiarism and questions about some of his achievements. He had denied the claims.

Liverpool John Moores University - which awarded Arday his PhD in 2015 - concluded that he had not plagiarised work.

The row first erupted after another academic - self-defined "race realist" Nathan Cofnas, who was sacked from his Cambridge role in 2024 - said he found numerous instances of plagiarism in the professor's work. Cofnas's post had been terminated amid a backlash to his view that under a true meritocracy black people would "disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment".

Lord Woolley told BBC Radio 4's Broadcasting House programme on Sunday he and a number of close friends had met Arday four days before he was found dead at a south London address.

He said Abbott and social activist Misan Harriman were among those who gathered to offer support as they had also experienced "horrible media attention".

He said Arday felt "hounded" and the relentless media coverage had been "a bloodsport".

"Diane said to him, she held his hand, and said we will help you get through this," he added.

"But on that day, we saw a man half his body weight and desperate beyond belief."

Lord Woolley said issues of plagiarism were constant in academia and that a number of individuals, who had been accused of plagiarism had not been subjected to the attention Arday had received.

"We have to ask this question, we have to talk about - which a lot of people don't want to talk about, is racism. You have to look at negatively differential treatment."

On 6 August Cambridge announced an independent investigation into Arday's appointment.

It is understood the university does not feel it right to decide on whether to proceed with its investigation.

But one of the academic's friends, Sir Simon Baron-Cohen, told Times Radio on Sunday it should go ahead to "see what we learn from it" because "this is the whole purpose of investigations".

A University of Cambridge spokesperson told the BBC that during his time at the university, Arday had received a range of support in relation to his physical and mental well-being, including counselling and support and advice.

"Our support continued in the face of intense public and media scrutiny and after his resignation," they added.

Cambridge celebrated Arday's appointment as a young black professor, one of a tiny and visible minority in academia. Only one per cent of professors in UK universities are black, making each appointment hugely significant.

More than Â£90,000 has now been raised for Arday's family, after Windrush campaigner Sir Patrick Vernon, who is also among the signatories to the petition, launched a fundraiser.

A vigil organised by group Stand Up To Racism is set to take place on Monday evening in Trafalgar Square.

News.title: History for Hunt and Asher-Smith in golden finish for GB
News.content:
Amy Hunt and Dina Asher-Smith made history and Georgia Hunter Bell claimed a commanding 1500m gold in a spectacular finish for Great Britain at the European Championships.

Sprint sensation Hunt held up four fingers to the camera after holding off Germany's challenge on the home straight of the mixed 4x100m relay as another sell-out crowd roared the 24-year-old on to an unprecedented fourth gold in Birmingham.

The world silver medallist completed victory for the quartet in a European record 39.97 seconds to add to her triumphs in the 100m, 200m and women's 4x100m in the past seven days.

"Oh my gosh, I am over the moon. I think to finish it off with some of my best friends in the sport is incredible," Hunt told BBC Sport.

With her eighth gold and 11th medal overall, Asher-Smith is unparalleled as the most successful athlete in the competition's 92-year history, with a team also featuring Jeremiah Azu and Zharnel Hughes extending the hosts' domination of the sprint events.

Hunter Bell expertly controlled the women's 1500m final before bursting clear to continue her golden year by adding to world indoor and Commonwealth glory.

That represented the 32-year-old's seventh international medal in two years as she continues to build momentum on her fairytale return to the sport which she quit for five years following a promising junior career.

News.title: Changing pubs into homes to be made harder under new rules
News.content:
The Campaign for Real Ale has previously said that pubs are being "lost forever to conversion or demolition as developers look to cash in on the desirable locations and unique architecture of pubs and social clubs".

The British Beer and Pub Association and UKHospitality have also campaigned against pub closures, with both largely blaming tax rises and other costs.

Allen Simpson, chief executive of UKHospitality, said: "The biggest issue facing hospitality businesses is costs like VAT and business rates pushing pubs out of business in the first place.

"Anything that makes it harder to take these important assets away from their communities has to be welcomed, but the government should focus on continuing its strong start on fixing the harm done to hospitality over the past two years."

In July, the Labour government said pubs, social clubs and live music venues in England will be given a 20% cut to business rates on top of rates relief announced in January.

The NPPF update being published Monday also includes default approval for homes being built around railway stations in England in an attempt to increase housebuilding numbers.

Housing Secretary Angela Rayner said: "By unlocking thousands of homes around well-connected transport hubs, we're helping people live closer to work, school and the services they rely on, while backing local businesses and driving growth in our communities."

The update also means that some groups will no longer need to be consulted on housing development plans as part of the process of getting permission.

The Gardens Trust, a parks and gardens heritage and conversion charity, called the decision to remove its role as a statutory consultee "devastating".

It said it devalued parks and gardens and "makes them vulnerable to poorly informed development".

Under the changes, the Gardens Trust and Theatres Trust will still be notified of relevant applications and Sport England will continue to advise on significant cases.

Labour has set a target to build 1.5 million homes by 2029. According to official data, external, it has so far built 392,000 homes in England since coming into power in July 2024.

Shadow housing secretary Sir James Cleverly said Labour is "failing abysmally" to meet their target because of taxes and red tape.

"To try to fix their own mess, Labour are planning a power grab, seizing control from local communities and forcing them to accept development in the wrong areas because Labour won't build in the right areas," he added.

News.title: 'I want my brother back' - Tupac’s brother tells BBC murder trial won’t bring justice
News.content:
The BBC's Shaimaa Khalil sat down with Mopreme Shakur, Tupac Shakur's stepbrother, ahead of opening statements on Monday in trial of the man accused of killing the rapper.

During the interview, Mopreme reflected on Tupac's legacy 30 years after his death, recalled the night of the shooting, and shared what it was like to grow up alongside one of the most influential figures in hip-hop.

Read more about the case here.

News.title: Reform UK benefits ban for foreign nationals would include EU citizens
News.content:
It is the latest announcement ahead of a speech on Monday by Reform's shadow chancellor Robert Jenrick to formally unveil the party's welfare plans.

"Forcing British workers to pay for the benefits of foreigners is not just economically illiterate but plain immoral," Jenrick said in a statement.

"People are more than happy to support their neighbours in hard times, but the British taxpayer cannot afford to subsidise everyone on the planet, especially those who have not paid in."

This year the government expects, external to spend a total of Â£322bn on welfare in Great Britain, or 10.6% of GDP, just over half of which goes to pensioners.

Reform says it has spent six months drawing up a 50-page plan that it claims will save a total of Â£50bn a year.

On Saturday, the party said it would replace the disability payments system, Pip, if it entered Number 10 at the next election.

The latest proposals would ban foreign nationals from almost all welfare payments including housing benefit, pension credit, jobseeker's allowance, child benefit, free childcare and disability benefits.

Only a small number of exemptions would apply, including the war widows pension and Armed Forces compensation.

The party had previously pledged to ban foreign nationals from claiming Universal Credit.

News.title: People who fled Stourbridge fires start to return home
News.content:
People who had to flee their houses during the devastating Stourbridge fires are starting to return home, as a firefighter said it was "a miracle no one has died".

Many families are only just discovering the extent of damage to their homes as West Midlands Fire Service allowed some behind the cordon after three days.

Nineteen properties across five streets have been fully destroyed. Eight households have been able to view the shells of their former homes.

Aerial images of the scene appear to show some houses have remained entirely intact while those next to them have been burnt to the ground.

Residents of Brunswick Gate, Landsgate, Ounty John Lane, Quarry Park Road and Racecourse Lane were asked to gather to speak to fire chiefs one by one.

They then learned if it was safe to return or if their home needed significant repairs or had been lost entirely.

Earlier, Dudley Council's chief executive Balvinder Heran said 96 evacuated houses had escaped damage with 85 families able to return.

Thirteen households whose properties were damaged by fire have also been able to go back home.

News.title: Somali man charged with attempted murder at Surrey asylum hotel
News.content:
Police have charged a man with attempted murder at a hotel used to house asylum seekers in Stanwell.

Armed officers were dispatched to the Stanwell Hotel, near Heathrow Airport, on Saturday evening over reports a man had been stabbed, Surrey Police said in a statement.

Paramedics took the victim, a hotel staff member in his 30s, to hospital with life-threatening injuries. He is now in a stable condition, police wrote in the latest update.

Police said that 22-year-old Somali national Abdifatah Yusuf Adani remains in custody and is due to face one charge of attempted murder when he appears at Staines Magistrates Court on Monday morning.

"There remains a heightened police presence in the area," the police said in a statement shared on Sunday night.

Earlier on Saturday, Detective Superintendent Kate Hyder of Surrey Police said "we understand this incident has caused concern within the local community, and I encourage you to speak to local officers."

Police said they are not pursuing anyone else connected to the incident.

News.title: UK-made drones strike targets inside Russia
News.content:
British-made drones are being used to strike targets in Russia for the first time.

The drones, built by two separate British companies, have been used in mainland Russia in widespread and successful targeting of military and industrial targets, including refineries and warehouses of online retailer Wildberries.

The strikes, first reported by the Sunday Times, external, are said to have caused more than Â£35bn in economic damage. A well-placed military source confirmed to the BBC the UK drones had been used.

British manufactured Storm Shadow missiles had earlier been used in the conflict, although this new phase is having a far more decisive impact.

Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova has previously said drones using UK components and configurations have been used to attack Russian territory, including a fuel depot in the Kamensky District of the Rostov Region.

In April, the Ministry of Defence (MoD) announced it would supply Ukraine tens of thousands of drones, including long-range strike devices, in its biggest ever package.

The MoD said its support for Ukraine is "unwavering" and would stand by its ally "until it wins".

A spokesperson said: "We are committed to providing the equipment Ukraine needs to defend itself against Putin's illegal invasion.

"This includes over 150,000 drones this year, cutting-edge Stone Cloak devices that hinder Russian air defences and innovative low-cost cruise missiles."

On Sunday, Moscow's mayor said about 600 Ukrainian drones were launched towards the city overnight, with roughly a third of the drones being destroyed, and three people were injured.

A warehouse belonging to Russian online retailer Wildberries was hit.

Wildberries, known as Russia's version of Amazon, has been repeatedly targeted since July.

Kyiv said at the time it was targeting logistics hubs used by Russians to buy military equipment and disrupting supplies to the Russian army.

News.title: Soldiers praised for 'phenomenal job' helping crews tackle wildfires
News.content:
In south Wales, about 14 separate fires were being tackled by crews on Sunday.

Mid and West Wales Fire Rescue and Service said crews were dealing with blazes at Rhandirmwyn and Ammanford in Carmarthenshire and Hay-on-Wye and Brecon in Powys on Sunday.

They have also attended fires in Gorseinon, Swansea, and Tenby, Pembrokeshire, as well as an incident involving smoke in Llanelli, Carmarthenshire.

Fire service manager, Geraint Thomas, described tree-height flames spreading in a pine forest in the Rhandirmwyn area of Carmarthenshire.

He said the perimeter of the fire expanded to 480 hectares with areas of broadleaved woodland, mountain moorland as well as pine forest burning within it.

"It's really challenging terrain in places," he said.

"The majority of the fire is quite deep-seated in the pine forest. We were limited in what we could see."

The Mid and West Wales Fire and Rescue Service area manager said the flames are now under control thanks largely to much cooler conditions on Friday.

Chris Bryant, MP for Rhondda and Ogmore, said a fire in Treherbert, Rhondda Cynon Taf, had been "appalling" and he thanked crews from London who had provided assistance.

"Thankfully, there are fire engines from all over the UK and two helicopters have been in place all afternoon.

"I'm immensely impressed by the fire workers. But this can't be our new normal," he said, in a post on X, external on Saturday.

Monahan praised the Royal Logistics Corps and Royal Engineers in ensuring crews had water to tackle the fires.

"The Welsh water system is under pressure, so they're moving vast quantities of water from areas that we have it into areas where we're fighting the fire, so that we don't put too much pressure on the water system," he said.

"That's something people probably aren't aware of."

He also said the national emergency fire alert issued by the UK government to people's mobile phones in England and Wales on Friday was "absolutely necessary".

But he expressed disappointment that some people still did not appreciate the dangers.

"Even after that transmission, I stopped and found someone who was burning tyres underneath a tree.

"This is irresponsible behaviour," he said.

News.title: Sinn Féin condemn burning of images of first minister on Derry bonfire
News.content:
Sinn FÃ©in has condemned the burning of images of First Minister Michelle O'Neill on a bonfire in Londonderry as "anti-democratic" and "sectarian".

On Saturday, a bonfire, from which almost 500 pallets were removed during the week, was set on fire beside a road in the Bogside area.

Photos of O'Neill, as well as union jacks, Israeli flags, Parachute Regiment, Somme Remembrance and Northern Ireland flags were attached to the bonfire.

Police are treating the burning of the effigies and materials as sectarian-motivated hate crimes.

In a post on social media, O'Neill said she would "not be deterred, distracted or intimidated".

"I will continue to call out sectarianism, anti-community activity and destruction wherever it comes from.

"These bonfires are a blight on our community," she said.

Secretary of State for Northern Ireland Sir Chris Bryant said it was "wrong and I strongly condemn it".

"Hatred like that only takes us back to the past - which is not what the vast majority of people in Northern Ireland want."

North Belfast MP John Finucane said these bonfires were "hate filled sectarianism" and "the very antithesis of Irish republicanism".

Youths placed pallets near the bottom of the Lecky Road flyover and set fire to it just before 23:00 BST.

Two other bonfires in the Creggan and Top of the Hill areas of the city also had flags and effigies placed on them before being set alight.

News.title: Elgin man found after going missing in Rome on first night of holiday
News.content:
A 56-year-old man from Moray who went missing in Rome on the first night of his holiday has been found, according to his family.

Colin Ross had just arrived in the Italian capital with partner Anabella Mcallister, when he disappeared up a side street near the Pantheon at about 22:00 on Friday evening.

Posting on social media, Mcallister said Ross, from Elgin, had become unsteady due to his medication and the heat, and did not have his phone or wallet with him.

His daughter later told STV News, external that he'd been found injured "walking around in the street" but "somehow made it back".

After Ross went missing, Mcallister said online that "he was in a bit of an unsteady state due to medication and heat."

She added that as she stopped to take a photograph, her fiancÃ© went up a side street and by the time she had followed him he had disappeared.

Earlier, a spokesperson for the Foreign Office said it was supporting the family of a British man missing in Italy and was in touch with the local authorities.

BBC Scotland News has contacted Italy's state police for comment.

News.title: Watch moment police arrest wanted man while he slept on roof
News.content:
A stand-off involving a wanted man was brought to an end when police arrested him while he slept on a roof.

Greater Manchester Police (GMP) said emergency services had responded to an incident at a property on Reservoir Street in Salford, spending two days at the scene.

Footage shows officers from the force's tactical unit gently resting a ladder against the roof of a back porch, with an officer then grabbing the man while he was sleeping.

A struggle ensues and the man is pulled down, with his trousers appearing to fall down, before he is arrested by officers in the garden of the property.

Two police officers suffered minor injuries during the incident on Saturday.

GMP said it was asked by another force to arrest the man who was wanted on recall to prison for other matters.

The force said a 37-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of causing public nuisance, criminal damage, public order offences, burglary and assaulting two police officers.

He remains in police custody.

Det Ch Insp Helen Bagnall said: "During two days of disruption to the local community, we worked continuously with our partners to bring this matter to a safe conclusion.

"This was an extensive use of vital policing resources and clearly demonstrates the dangers our officers face on a daily basis in order to protect the people of Greater Manchester."

She thanked the people of Salford for their "patience and understanding" while emergency services dealt with the incident, adding some properties had been damaged as a result of the man's actions.

She said the force would work with partners to ensure affected residents would be supported.

News.title: Man with dementia given days to leave Sweden
News.content:
Torossian said the situation had been "awful" and "traumatic" for the family.

"I'm just worried that if the police go in and try and take him, how is that going to affect my dad. We just want him to have some dignity," she said.

"We want him to be treated like someone - he's very vulnerable, and I just feel that this is really ruthless and harsh."

Torossian said doctors had advised the Swedish authorities the process of moving Mason to the UK would pose a "danger to his life".

When the UK left the European Union (EU) on 31 January 2020, British citizens stopped being EU citizens, which meant they could no longer stay in Sweden with right of residence status.

During a transitional period, British citizens could apply for residence status under a withdrawal agreement between the UK and the EU - which ended on 31 December 2021.

Torossian explained due to Mason's health conditions, a 'god man' - a legally appointed trustee - was given power of attorney to look after her dad's affairs.

Documents from the Swedish Migration Agency, seen by the BBC, state an application for permanent residency for Mason was made on 21 December 2021.

However, it was refused on the grounds documents showing he met the grounds for residency were not submitted.

Fox News presenter Joey Jones is under fire following a three-minute on-air outburst targeting service members deployed aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln who recently voiced concerns about deteriorating shipboard conditions.

Sailors and their families have complained about conditions, including the food, on the ship given its deployment for more than 200 days. The carrier has been in the Middle East helping in Donald Trump’s war in Iran. Administration officials, including the president, have dismissed concerns about the conditions.

“How weak are you?” Jones asked while co-hosting Fox News’s “The Big Weekend Show” on Saturday, reacting to a segment that originally aired Thursday on CNN.

“On TV, complaining about tuna and noodles?” Jones said. “I’m sorry, you volunteered to serve your country. You can come back, get out of the military, and do like all of these Democrat veterans and complain about it and make commercials and be a sellout if you want to.”

On social media, critics immediately turned the host’s own framing against him.

“Put him on that ship for the same length of time under similar conditions,” user Darryl Brown posted on X.

open image in gallery A Fox News host is facing criticism after launching a three-minute tirade against service members aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln who spoke out about deteriorating conditions at sea ( Reuters )

Another commentator, Doan Jeannot, called the remarks “hilarious given that MAGA is the truest personification of weakness.”

The host’s remarks followed an anonymous interview with a sailor stationed on the aircraft carrier, which has been in the Middle East since Nov. 21, 2025. It was recently announced that the ship would return home after more than 250 days.

“I would say morale’s pretty low, and not just in the division, like in the ship entirely,” the service member told CNN, adding that crew members were running low on food. “I mean at some points in the day it would just be about noodles and tuna mixed in together, and that was it … sometimes you get a corndog, sometimes you get a hot dog.”

Following the clip, Jones, a former Marine Corps staff sergeant who lost both legs to an improvised explosive device in Afghanistan in 2010, drew comparisons to his own military service.

“To sit there and say that it was terrible because you had a corn dog and a hot dog?” Jones said. “I would’ve traded a block of C-4 to the Taliban for a hot dog by about July 2010. I just do not understand the mentality.”

Viewers quickly condemned the network’s tone toward deployed personnel.

“Good job Fox News, let's shame service members,” X user @crimephotosss wrote in response.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump has dismissed concerns about the conditions on the USS Abraham Lincoln ( Getty Images )

“So now they’ve successfully dehumanized all Hispanics, Democrats and now they’re going after the military,” another X user, Ann Panel, wrote. “Making fun of our service men and women is absolutely shocking. These people go out and are willing to sacrifice their lives for this country.”

The host's remarks come as the carrier strike group faces growing concern following reports of severe supply shortages, declining mental health and incidents of sailors jumping overboard, according to Stars and Stripes.

Top administration officials have consistently downplayed the reported hardships aboard the vessel.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth defended the military’s logistics during a visit to Panama, telling reporters: “We make sure every ship, every crew, every captain has everything we can provide them at every single moment. Some deployments are longer than others, and I have more respect and gratitude for those sailors than anybody. What they do in those high seas in those austere conditions with less port calls — it’s incredible.”

Speaking at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland, President Donald Trump flatly disputed accounts of sailors jumping into the ocean.

“No, they’re not,” Trump said when asked about the reports. “That ship is moving right now, or very shortly, and it’s being replaced with another very similar ship.”

British sprinter Amy Hunt was delighted to have succeeded beyond her wildest dreams after becoming the first athlete to win four gold medals at a single European Championships.

The 24-year-old world silver 200m medallist sealed her unprecedented quadruple in the inaugural mixed 4x100m relay final in front of a sold-out crowd at the Alexander Stadium to conclude a six-medal super Sunday in Birmingham.

Dina Asher-Smith also moved to the outright top of the European Athletics Championships all-time list with her 11th medal, and silver for Matt Hudson-Smith in the men’s 4x400m relay, bringing the hometown hero to nine, made him the outright most-decorated man in the history of the European Championships, and there was also gold for Georgia Hunter Bell in the 1500m final.

open image in gallery Jeremiah Azu (left), Dina Asher-Smith, Zharnel Hughes, (2nd left) Amy Hunt (right) with their gold medals (Mike Egerton/PA) ( PA Wire )

“Oh my gosh, (I feel) just sensational!” said Hunt. “I think it surpassed my expectations for myself at this champs, not in terms of just the golds, but how I’ve handled myself, how I’ve handled all the pressure, the attention, the recovery, the discipline of it all.

“Not getting too caught up in the highs and staying kind of true to myself, keeping humble and keeping my foot on the gas the whole way through the week. Seven races in seven days is no easy feat.”

Jeremiah Azu, Asher-Smith, Zharnel Hughes and Hunt beat Germany and Spain in 39.97s.

Asher-Smith joined Polish sprinter Irena Szewinska on 10 European medals with women’s 4×100 relay triumph on Saturday after also collecting 200m bronze earlier in the week, although she already had two more golds to her name.

open image in gallery Dina Asher-Smith (right) celebrates her 11th European Championship medal (Martin Rickett/PA) ( PA Wire )

With Sunday’s addition, the British record-holder is now up to eight European golds, and is the lone athlete with 11 medals overall.

“It hasn’t sunk in at all,” she said, when asked about her achievement. “At this point in my career, I’m just having fun. I’m just seeing what can be maxed out because I’m fortunate enough to stand on the line, and I don’t really have much to prove. I’d like an Olympic gold, but that’s kind of the only thing that’s on my bucket list.

“Being able to kind of come here and just kind of have fun and do some more events is a privilege. It’s definitely a privilege.”

The mixed 4×100 relay made its European Championships debut in Birmingham, opening the possibility for the ambitious Hunt to set her sights on four titles on home soil after clinching a sprint double, then women’s 4x100m gold.

open image in gallery Abbie Donnelly won marathon bronze (Mike Egerton/PA) ( PA Wire )

Hunt and Asher-Smith confirmed that they were not unduly affected by security measures at the venue on Saturday night, when it was previously understood that all of the teams in that evening session’s two relays were unable to leave on time due to security measures as a result of a police incident.

The women’s 4x400m relay quartet of Yemi Mary-John, Lina Nielsen, Nicole Yeargin and Emily Newnham struck silver, while their men’s counterparts, Hudson-Smith, Toby Harries, Ben Jeffries and Dobson finished three one hundredths of a second behind Italy in the competition’s closing race.

Jazmin Sawyers also snatched silver in the long jump, and Abbie Donnelly became the first British woman to win a marathon medal at the European Championships, with bronze.

Researchers have welcomed a new antimalarial compound as "an exciting step forward" in the global fight against the disease.

Discovered by a team at the University of Dundee, the molecule has the potential to streamline dosing schedules for both prevention and treatment.

Malaria is a severe mosquito-borne illness that mostly affects people living in tropical countries.

Global statistics from 2024 show an estimated 282 million malaria cases and 610,000 deaths, with numbers escalating partly due to increasing resistance to current drugs.

open image in gallery The compound was discovered by researchers at the University of Dundee, who said it has the potential to simplify dosing regimens for the treatment and prevention of the illness ( Jason Baxter/Alamy/PA )

The compound, called cabamiquine, is described as a "novel drug-like molecule" that can be administered in a single dose.

Early-stage trial results showed that when combined with the existing drug pyronaridine, the treatment proved effective and demonstrated a favourable safety profile in adults and teenagers.

The findings support further testing of the combined therapy in larger trials and among paediatric patients.

Dr Beatriz Baragana, a member of the Dundee University team that discovered cabamiquine, said: "This is an exciting step forward for a compound which has great potential to simplify dosing regimens for malaria, a disease which causes hundreds of thousands of deaths every year.

"All of the initial work that ultimately resulted in the discovery of cabamiquine was performed here in Dundee, with support and funding from Medicines for Malaria Venture (MMV).

"We are delighted to see how the compound, when administered with pyronaridine, is progressing into a potential malaria medicine, giving hope to the millions of people affected by malaria every year."

Professor Ian Gilbert is head of the University of Dundee’s drug discovery unit, which spearheaded the breakthrough.

The division collaborates with scientific partners to turn biological research into candidate drugs addressing unmet medical needs.

Prof Gilbert said: "The benefits of this compound are not only that it looks to be effective, with a good benefit/risk profile, but it can also be delivered in a single dose, which is an important factor when you are treating a disease that occurs commonly in areas where consistent delivery of healthcare can be challenging."

Following scientific and financial support from MMV, the organisation now plans to progress cabamiquine-pyronaridine into further development.

Paul Willis, vice president of drug discovery and preclinical safety at MMV, said: "Novel treatment and prevention regimens are urgently needed with simplified dosing to enable effective case management and to support long-term malaria control and elimination goals."

The study's findings were published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases.

Conducted by pharmaceutical firm Merck as part of the PAMAfrica consortium, the trial was co-funded by the EDCTP2 Programme, with support from the European Union and the Swedish International Development Co-operation Agency.

Householders are moving away from minimalist grey interiors to embrace warmer tones, according to paint brand Lick.

The shift comes as the business reported strong sales growth over the first half of the year, bucking a broader slowdown across the home improvement sector.

Boss Lucas London explained that the company has benefited as high mortgage rates continue to discourage people from moving, leading shoppers to focus on making their current homes more cosy.

The brand noted particularly strong demand for green and pink paint over the last year.

Shades of green proved to be its most popular, representing 17.4 per cent of sales during the past 12 months. Meanwhile, pink paint also saw strengthening demand, accounting for 13.9 per cent of sales, up from 12.5 per cent a year earlier.

It comes as previous demand for grey interiors, which had been buoyed by influencers such as Mrs Hinch, continued to crater.

Homeowners are ditching grey interiors amid a shift away from minimalism towards warmer tones, according to paint brand Lick ( PA )

Demand for grey paint tumbled in half to only 2.3 per cent of sales as part of the shift away from cooler, minimalist styles.

Nevertheless, white paint remained popular over the year and neutral tones beige and taupe saw an increase in sales.

The chief executive and co-founder of the brand said it has seen overall demand for its paint remain robust despite wider consumer spending pressures.

Mr London suggested he believes the group has benefited from having a lower price point than traditional upmarket paid brands.

“I think customers doing DIY have found our paint relatively affordable,” he said.

“For the first half sales were up 51 per cent, so that’s showing that we’re very strong and outperforming the market.

“People are really discerning about the quality but also keen to marry that up with an affordable price point right now, they are always thinking about value.”

Andy Burnham’s decision on whether to approve the controversial Jackdaw and Rosebank oil and gas fields could be the difference between “life and death” for the North Sea industry, the Scottish Conservatives have said.

A public consultation on Rosebank – the largest untapped oil field in the North Sea, 80 miles north west of Shetland – closes on Monday.

A similar exercise for the planned Jackdaw gas field, about 150 miles east of Aberdeen, finished on August 10.

open image in gallery Conservative energy minister and shadow Scottish secretary Andrew Bowie (Euan Cherry/PA) ( PA Wire )

Production at both fields had been approved by the previous Conservative government, but those decisions were quashed after a legal challenge by Greenpeace, leaving Labour ministers to decide whether drilling should go ahead.

Conservative energy minister and shadow Scottish secretary Andrew Bowie said: “Labour’s decision on both Jackdaw and Rosebank could be the difference between life and death for an industry that has supported the UK for generations.

“The absurd North Sea energy policy of both Westminster and Holyrood governments risks bringing a premature end to our oil and gas sector as we know it.

“I am absolutely positive that the results of both consultations will send a clear message to Andy Burnham to stop the small talk and get Britain drilling again.”

Industry body Offshore Energies UK (OEUK) has said Rosebank and Jackdaw would support a peak of more than 3,500 jobs during construction, and 880 jobs externally throughout during their lifespans.

open image in gallery (PA Graphics) ( PA Graphics )

Mr Bowie said: “These oil and gas fields, which the Conservatives have supported from the very beginning, will help shape the lives of thousands of North Sea workers for years to come.

“BP’s decision to end its North Sea operations must be the catalyst for Labour to get Jackdaw and Rosebank up and running as a matter of urgency.

“Anything other than approving these fields will threaten our energy security, cost thousands of jobs, and move our world-leading oil and gas industry one step closer to extinction.”

In a letter seen by the Press Association, Stop Climate Chaos Scotland (SCCS) – a campaign group made up of more than 70 organisations with around a million supporters – said the new Prime Minister must block the proposed new developments.

It warned Mr Burnham and Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh that the “consequences of climate change are already being felt, through more extreme heat, drought, wildfires and growing risks to food insecurity”.

open image in gallery Campaigners outside the Department For Energy Security And Net Zero in Westminster (Yui Mok/PA) ( PA Wire )

The letter claimed that approving new fields such as Rosebank and Jackdaw is “not compatible with climate goals”.

The OEUK has said it recognises the threat of climate change, but the UK needs “realism” in its energy policy.

David Whitehouse, who leads OEUK, said: “Unprecedented heatwaves are reminding us that climate change is not a future threat but a present reality. The UK needs both urgency and realism in its energy policy. That means accelerating renewable energy and also being honest about today’s energy system.

“The reality is that oil and gas still provide around 75% of the UK’s energy, keeping our cars moving, planes flying, homes warm and industries running.

“If we do not produce this oil and gas here with lower emissions under one of the most tightly regulated regimes in the world, we do not end demand. It just means more imported oil and gas – often with a higher carbon footprint, while more jobs, taxes and industrial value are shifted overseas. The Government must be honest about this.”

A DESNZ spokesperson said: “The North Sea remains a vital national asset, supporting jobs, growth and the UK’s energy security.

“We are clear that oil and gas will continue to play an important role in our energy system for decades to come, alongside transitioning to clean power to protect jobs and tackle the climate crisis.”

News.title: Average price tag on a home plunges by £7,360 in August – Rightmove
News.content:

The average price tag on a home coming on the market nosedived by more than £7,000 in August, according to figures from a property website.

Rightmove has also downgraded its house price forecast for 2026 from a 2% increase to a change of between zero and a 2% fall in average new seller asking prices over the year as a whole.

It said the average newly listed asking price in August fell by 2.0% or £7,360 month-on-month, marking the biggest August price fall since 2018.

Prices usually fall in the month of August but this is a much bigger drop than the 10-year average of 1.3%, the website said.

Across Britain, the average asking price for a home in August is £364,999.

The price is 1.0% lower than a year earlier, marking the biggest annual drop since December 2023.

The number of available homes for sale is also at a 12-year high for this time of year, and when combined with the traditionally quiet summer holiday period, this has led to lower price expectations from sellers, the website said.

The average figure masks an increasingly divided regional picture for property price growth, Rightmove said.

In the North West of England, the average asking price is up by 1.9% annually but in London it has fallen by 3.1%.

open image in gallery Rightmove’s map shows average asking prices across Britain (Rightmove/PA)

Get a free fractional share worth up to £100.

Capital at risk. Terms and conditions apply. Go to website 

Colleen Babcock, a property expert at Rightmove, said: “This month’s larger-than-usual August price drop is a sign that many sellers are recognising the reality of the market and pricing much more competitively from day one.

“Buyers have the widest choice of homes for sale at this time of year in more than a decade, so standing out on price for the right reasons is hugely important.”

She added: “One tactic some sellers are using when considering lower offers on their home is to also make a lower offer themselves on their onwards purchase, to see if they can make up the difference.”

Although buying activity is still around 10% below last year’s level, Rightmove said it had seen a “mini bounce” in buyer demand since Andy Burnham became Prime Minister.

But it said the changing picture for mortgage rates, alongside geopolitical uncertainty and the Budget in October were creating housing market uncertainty.

Ms Babcock added: “The mini Burnham bounce and some renewed general optimism have brought a degree of improvement to the market as a whole in recent weeks.

“Whether that develops into a more sustained recovery will likely depend on confidence, mortgage rates and the new Chancellor’s first Budget this autumn.”

Marc von Grundherr, director of Benham and Reeves, said: “There’s no denying that London is having a more challenging year than many other parts of the country and affordability is at the heart of it.”

He added: “However, I wouldn’t characterise the London market as being in any sort of serious decline. What we’re seeing is a much more price-sensitive market and sellers who acknowledge that are still finding buyers.”

Jeremy Leaf, a north London estate agent said: “Although asking prices are not selling prices but often reflect owners’, or agents’, aspirational starting points, these figures help demonstrate how difficult it has become to attract genuine buyers.”

Meanwhile, a lettings index from property firm Hamptons, for the month of July, indicated that some landlords are seeing opportunities to snap up properties in the slower sales market.

It found that 56% of investor offers in July were at least 10% below the initial asking price – rising to 63% among landlords paying in cash.

It said 27% of these lower offers from investors were accepted in July 2026, compared with just 18% in July 2025.

The analysis of offers used data from the Connells Group and covered England and Wales.

Hamptons also released rental price figures, covering Britain, and also using data from Connells Group. The index is based on achieved rather than advertised rents.

It said the average monthly rental price for a newly-let home jumped by 1.9% annually in July, marking the fastest pace of rental growth recorded for new lets in 19 months. The average monthly rent on a newly-let home was £1,401.

David Fell, lead analyst at Hamptons, said: “When the market slows, seasoned investors rarely stand on the sidelines for long.

“With homes taking longer to sell and chains proving fragile, landlords are using their liquidity and chain-free status to maximise their leverage when it comes to agreeing a price.”

He added: “While higher borrowing costs continue to weigh on investment returns, landlords with cash or low levels of borrowing are finding that a slower market is creating opportunities to purchase at significantly lower prices than would have been possible a few years ago.”

Mr Fell said of the rental price increases: “Although these hikes may not be as large as in previous peak years, for landlords, the re-emergence of an upward trajectory in rents provides a counterweight to higher borrowing costs.”

Here are average rental prices per month on newly-let homes and the annual change, according to Hamptons:

News.content:

Confiscations of dangerous e-bikes by police forces across the UK have risen by 83 per cent over a single year following targeted operations.

Data obtained by the Press Association through freedom-of-information requests reveals that 7,049 machines were seized in the 12 months to 19 May, compared with 3,858 in the previous period.

The sharp increase has driven calls from police, politicians and charities for updated legislation to address non-compliant models linked to fatalities and severe injuries.

Sergeant Stuart Ford, who heads the City of London Police cycle team, branded illegal e-bikes "a menace".

Julie Minns, Labour MP for Carlisle, is pushing for a ban on sales of illegal e-bikes and conversion kits, describing them as the "perfect accessory to phone theft, mugging and drug dealing". She called on Andy Burnham’s Government to designate them an "unsafe product".

During a recent crackdown in Cardiff, South Wales Police arrested four riders on suspicion of drug offences after a man in his 20s was found carrying 33 wraps of heroin and crack cocaine worth roughly £1,000.

open image in gallery Police seizures of e-bikes soared by 83 per cent in a year, an investigation has found ( PA )

Under UK law, legal e-bikes are known as electrically assisted pedal cycles (EAPCs) and must meet certain safety regulations such as their electric motor having a maximum power output of 250 watts and cutting out when a speed of 15.5mph is reached.

Many illegal e-bikes confiscated by police have been modified to travel much faster, with some exceeding 70mph.

Non-compliant machines are effectively electric mopeds or motorbikes, which must be registered, taxed and insured.

While major retailers sell thousands of legal e-bikes every year, many illegal machines are bought on the internet.

Kits which add an electronic motor to a conventional bike are available online for under £300.

As well as being used for crime, illegal e-bikes are also often used for legitimate journeys such as food deliveries and commuting.

Thirty-one police forces out of 45 across the UK provided comparable data after PA’s freedom-of-information requests.

The Metropolitan Police was the force which seized the most e-bikes in the year to 19 May, with 2,367.

That was ahead of Leicestershire Police (661), Police Scotland (585) and Thames Valley Police (425).

The 11 forces which saw seizures more than double year on year were Devon and Cornwall, Dorset, Hampshire, Leicestershire, Lincolnshire, Northamptonshire, Northumbria, South Yorkshire, Suffolk, Thames Valley and the Police Service of Northern Ireland.

Wiltshire Police said half of its seizures were recorded in Swindon, the town which Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander’s constituency covers.

Last month, the Met carried out an operation to catch illegal e-bike users near Tottenham Court Road station in London’s West End – a hotspot for phone theft and other street crime.

Speaking to PA at the scene, Commander Neerav Patel said Londonders were “fed-up of the criminal and antisocial use of e-bikes”.

The force has started using portable rolling road devices so officers can test an e-bike’s maximum speed using its motor to help them spot illegal machines.

City of London Police seized four of the machines in just half an hour last month.

Mr Ford said some illegal e-bikes are three times heavier than a conventional bike.

open image in gallery Sergeant Stuart Ford, who leads the cycle team at City of London Police, described illegal e-bikes as ‘a menace’

“If that was to hit a small child, it can cause serious injuries,” he warned.

Calling for new legislation to deal with illegal e-bike users, he added: “I would like to see specific laws around e-bikes brought in.”

Pedestrian safety charity Living Streets warned “the rise in e-bike use must not come at the expense of people walking” while the Royal National Institute of Blind People said e-bikes are “heavy, fast-moving, silent vehicles” that present a danger when “ridden carelessly”.

E-bikes have been behind a string of serious incidents:

Pedestrian Gloria Stephenson, 86, was knocked down and killed by an illegal e-bike on a zebra crossing in Sunderland in May last year.

A 10-year-old child was seriously injured after being hit by an e-bike on a pavement in Grimsby on 9 April.

A pregnant woman in her 30s struck by an e-bike while crossing a road in Poole, Dorset on 26 January was taken to hospital where she prematurely gave birth to a seriously ill baby.

A record 432 e-bike fires were reported in the UK last year, with brigades raising concerns about faulty batteries igniting while being charged.

A Government spokeswoman said: “Illegal e-bikes that can reach dangerous speeds have no place on our roads and pavements, and the rise in seizures shows the scale of the problem police are dealing with.

“That’s why we have strengthened police powers, changing the law so that officers no longer need to issue a warning before seizing these vehicles where they are used anti-socially.”

These tougher powers came into force on 29 June under the Crime and Policing Act 2026.
