Scotland begin their Nations League campaign with a trip to Slovenia on 26 September. Pocognoli’s first home game in charge will be Switzerland’s visit to Glasgow three days later.

Sports.title: Flemming’s dramatic Burnley double pegs back West Ham on Championship return
Sports.content:
There are many good reasons why Burnley and West Ham are performing as Premier League tribute acts, slumming it in the Championship with the hope of a shot at the limelight once more. They are two flawed teams, relegated because of chronic defects, and plenty were on show as West Ham blew a two-goal lead to start life on the second-tier circuit with an entertaining draw.

Zian Flemming’s late double secured a thoroughly deserved point for the hosts, who showed promise going forward but took far too long to find a clinical finish. Despite going two goals ahead through Maximilian Kilman and Manor Solomon, West Ham rarely looked comfortable as they sat back, something that eventually cost them.

“We did a very good first half,” Nuno Espírito Santo said. “We created a lot of situations we were able to control and stop Burnley. Not so good in the second half, but after we scored the second goal, I think we should have done better to keep the result.”

Nuno continued his career-long love of conservatism and his side were put under pressure early on, only surviving through Burnley’s poor decision-making and inept finishing. In addition to continuity in the dugout, West Ham can boast their captain, Jarrod Bowen, who committed to the club rather than seek a quick return to the top flight this summer. It was his corner that found Kilman at the back post after he lost Aaron Ramsey in the box.

Considering West Ham are favourites to go back up, this fortuitous lead should have been a foundation to build on, but little attempt was made to seek a second. They were passive for long periods, composed in possession, but Burnley were able to counter at speed through the midfield and cause problems, only to lack the composure to make the most of those situations.

Nuno tried to rectify the faltering midfield by sending on James Ward-Prowse for the anonymous Pablo, a player who has yet to find his level in England. It made no difference as Burnley came out the better side, pinning West Ham back repeatedly, but Flemming appeared destined to not score, finding the fans, goalkeeper, the inside of the post and Ollie Scarles on the line rather than the back of the net.

West Ham reminded everyone that they possess Premier League quality as Mohamadou Kanté made light work of Marcus Edwards on the right wing before pulling the ball back to Solomon to slam home from close range. This was their second and final shot on target, both leading to goals. Despite being second best, the visitors must have believed they were out of sight, by accident rather than design.

View image in fullscreen Maximilian Kilman gives West Ham the lead as he heads home Jarrod Bowen’s cross. Photograph: COLORSPORT/Alan Martin/Shutterstock

Flemming had other ideas as things finally clicked, aided by Scarles crudely taking out Edwards in the box, allowing the striker to settle his nerves after 83 minutes of near misses and create tension in the West Ham ranks. It worked as the visitors failed to clear a corner which Flemming swept home in the second minute of added time, further explaining why he has attracted transfer interest. Asked if Flemming will stay the Burnley manager, Nicky Hayen, who is desperate not to lose his talisman, said: “It does not help that he scored twice today.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Nuno will want more action in the transfer market after the record Championship signing of Arne Engels from Celtic on Saturday. A striker is much needed as Taty Castellanos made little impact, while the aforementioned Pablo does not give the impression of a man who will fire West Ham to promotion. The bench featured five academy graduates, none of who Nuno felt comfortable bringing on, which says a lot. “The club knows the targets and the needs of the team. [We are] working very hard and trying to get the bodies in as soon as possible,” Nuno said. “We need especially in the offensive part of the team.”

Hayen, celebrating his 46th birthday, took his team on a lap of honour after his first league game in charge as he aims to build a relationship with supporters, who suffered through plenty of unwatchable football under his predecessor. “We showed resilience and that’s why I’m really satisfied for these boys because they worked really hard to change this game around and also how we did it,” Hayen said. “I’m pleased with the fans, how they supported us for 95 minutes. We invested a lot of time before this game into them because what we wanted was really to find the connection with them, that we made the promise that we bring energy into the stadium, that we keep on going for 95 minutes and this is exactly what we did.”

Sports.title: Premier League 2026-27 preview No 11: Hull City
Sports.content:
Guardian writers’ predicted position: 20th (NB: this is not necessarily Louise Taylor’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)

Last season’s position: 6th (Championship)

Prospects

It is no exaggeration to say that Hull’s playoff triumph in May was a shock. They had, after all, started the season as Championship relegation favourites and operated under a transfer embargo throughout the campaign. Moreover, they conceded 66 league goals, the fourth-highest, along the way. Now another minor miracle will surely be required if Premier League survival is to be secured.

Much may hinge on Oli McBurnie, the scorer of 19 goals last season, succeeding where he has struggled in the past and retaining his scoring touch in the top tier, but there is no lack of optimism in East Yorkshire. “Think about us like a volcano,” says Hull’s owner, Acun Ilicali. “It’s boiling right now and it’s going to erupt.”

Hull intend following Sunderland’s template last summer by making 14 new signings, albeit on a significantly smaller budget. So far 11 – Jack Butland, Hidemasa Morita, Matt Targett, Óscar Zambrano, Jens Hjertø-Dahl, Elliot Stroud, Konstantinos Tzolakis, Lucas Herrington, Joe Gelhardt, Lucas Gourna-Douath and the club record buy, the central defender Nobel Mendy, who has arrived from Rayo Vallecano for just over £20m – have arrived.

“The transfer market is very slow,” said the manager, Sergej Jakirovic, who covets the Sunderland striker Wilson Isidor and last season’s 23-goal Championship top scorer, Swansea’s Zan Vipotnik. “But, in the last seven days of the window, it will become very, very quick.”

His cause has been hindered by pre-season injuries, with perhaps the biggest blow involving an arm problem suffered by Butland. It threatens to keep the former Rangers goalkeeper, who had impressed in friendlies, out until Christmas. The consensus is that Hull will have long since become a lost cause by then, but, much as the impressive Jakirovic needs new faces and Premier League nous, he does hold one ace card. Hull boast an exceptionally powerful team spirit driven by exemplary on-field leaders, including the veteran central defender John Egan. Maybe, just maybe, it can, once again, transport them further than anyone believes possible.

Off-field picture

In June, the playoff winners faced kicking off the new Premier League season handicapped by a near certain six-point deduction. A club that spent last season under a two-window English Football League transfer embargo avoided it by selling their goalkeeper Ivor Pandur and midfielder Aidon Shehu to Rangers and Panathinaikos respectively for a combined £8.5m. Access to the fruits of the top tier’s broadcast deal has since made Hull a whole lot wealthier, but Ilicali has pledged not to risk the club’s future by overspending and, at the time of writing, has invested around £78m on the new players.

Owner-fan relationship

Unpredictable and slightly conflicted. Aidon Shehu, the Turkish sports reporter turned media mogul – who is on his fifth manager since taking control in early 2022 – was offered a wholesale welcome when he took over from the unpopular Allam family, but he now exerts much more of a polarising effect on supporters. If November 2022, when he treated 320 fans to an all-expenses-paid week’s holiday at a luxury resort hotel in Antalya represented a high point, a nadir arrived when late payments resulted in Hull being placed under a transfer embargo last season. Nonetheless, the playoff triumph ensures many are prepared to offer the 57-year-old the benefit of the doubt.

The manager

The Mostar-born, 49-year-old Jakirovic has Bosnian and Croatian citizenship and says his life was shaped by the 1990s Balkan war that broke out when he was 14. “It was life or death,” he has said. “It has made me the person I am today.” Shortly after his arrival from Turkey’s Kayserispor, in June 2025, Hull were placed under a transfer embargo, but, defying widespread predictions of imminent relegation, he led the team to sixth place before beating Middlesbrough in the Championship playoff final. A central midfielder or central defender in his playing days, the former Bosnia and Herzegovina international led Dinamo Zagreb to the Croatian League and Cup double in 2024.

Star signing

View image in fullscreen Hidemasa Morita applauds the Sporting fans during the Portuguese Cup final in May, his last appearance for the Lisbon club. Photograph: SPP Sport Press Photo/Alamy

The Japan defensive midfielder Hidemasa Morita joined from Sporting Lisbon after four trophy-laden years in Portugal. A fans’ favourite in Lisbon, he played regular Champions League football last season as Sporting reached the quarter-finals and has 40 senior international caps. Morita could have stayed in Lisbon, but opted not to renew his contract in order to experience Premier League football. Hull fended off competition from Ipswich for the signature of the 31-year-old who was a key part of the Japan squad at Qatar 2022. Morita is the second Japanese player to represent Hull and his amalgam of experience and quality in a key position promise to prove invaluable.

Stat attack

The strangest part of the Championship playoffs might not have been the Southampton spying scandal. Hull were second-bottom for expected points, 53.1, and would have been relegated if underlying performances determined results. It was remarkable tthey won promotion and it will be even more surprising if they make a serious fist of staying up.

Set for a breakthrough

The 22-year-old central defender Charlie Hughes was Hull’s young player of the year last season and his assurance in possession and excellent passing range are bound to catch all sorts of Premier League eyes. Helpfully, his ballplaying ability is matched by some equally impressive – and combative – defending. After spending his youth in the academies of Liverpool and Manchester City, Hughes joined Wigan, leaving for Hull last summer. An imposing blend of steel and silk, a defender also comfortable in central midfield will miss the start of the season after hernia surgery. Happily, Hughes is expected back by early autumn at the latest and appears integral to the team’s survival hopes.

World Cup impact

Not content with helping Hull win the most unexpected of promotions, the Canada winger Liam Millar headed across the Atlantic to the World Cup. He made three appearances at the tournament as they reached the knockout stage, losing to Morocco in the round of 16. Given his career seemed in real jeopardy when he suffered a serious knee injury shortly after joining Hull in 2024, inclusion in Canada’s squad represented the fulfilment of an unlikely looking dream. “It was an unbelievable experience,” said the 26-year-old. “I’ve never seen Canada the way it was, I’ve never seen so many red shirts in Vancouver and Toronto. We want to inspire the next generation and I think we did Canada proud.”

Sports.title: Nabizada stunner edges Watford past Southampton as ‘Spygate’ still looms large
Sports.content:
Southampton will have to get used to being barracked as they travel the Championship this autumn, the “Spygate” team set to be everyone’s favourite boo boys in the second tier. Certainly that was the case in Hertfordshire, with Watford fans and players alike beside themselves after a hard-fought victory, decided by two memorable first-half goals.

Tonda Eckert, the Southampton head coach, remains under investigation for his part in the Spygate affair and presented a subdued figure both during and after this contest. He insisted that his team were more united than ever after suffering the indignity of being removed from last season’s playoffs, “but it would be easier to say that after a victory”, Eckert acknowledged.

Watford paid tribute to Kenny Jackett before the match, the one-club legend and local boy hailed with two minutes of applause. This celebration of longevity and connection, with a Panini-inspired tifo tumbling down the stands, cut a contrast with the current operation, where Alessio Dionisi has become Watford’s 12th full-time manager in just the past five years.

“I am very tired and my team was too by the end,” said the Italian who was coaching Empoli in Serie B last season. Dionisi praised the attitude of his team – “I liked the mentality of my players, in every moment I saw one team working together,” he said. He also benefited from the Pozzo family’s multi-club network and the local academy in digging out a victory.

The Spain under-21 attacker Iker Bravo was one of several signings to make the familiar trek from “sister” club Udinese this summer, and he made his mark quickly, opening the scoring with a quite stunning solo goal in the 12th minute. It was all his own work and Bravo had to deploy a combination of skills to turn an innocuous situation into real danger. Looking to latch on to a long ball some 40 yards from goal, the 6ftplaymaker won the first header then, crucially, got a second touch with an outstretched toe to get the ball under control. Bravo then span immediately and drove at goal, pushing his way into the box before chopping right and getting off a low shot that Daniel Peretz got a hand to, butcould not keep out.

View image in fullscreen Watford’s Amin Nabizada jumps for joy after scoring their second goal against Southampton. Photograph: Peter Tarry/PA

A great way to start any season, the energy among the Vicarage Road crowd grew immediately and the home side went on to dominate the first half. They doubled their lead in the 29th minute with a moment to remember for 19-year-old academy graduate Amin Nabizada who exploited the same gaps on the left of the Southampton defence to run with the ball from his own half before finishing precisely from a tight angle. “Nabizada was emotional but after the first 10 minutes he played well,” Dionisi said. “When there is one mentality amongst the team, then it’s better for him too.”

Southampton had the better of the second half, taking advantage of a drop in tempo from the hosts to assert their interests. A spell of concerted possession in the 56th minute ended with Kuryu Matsuki pulling out wide, the young midfielder Cam Bragg moving unmarked into the half space and his shift left finding the Canada World Cup star Cyle Larin to poke home from 10 yards out.

Larin had a chance to equalise just two minutes later with a shot on the turn but Federico Ravaglia – another new signing to impress for the Hornets – turned the ball round the post. When Finn Azaz came on as a second-half substitute for the Saints he bought an inch to fire off a low drive that went just beyond the left hand post. As a succession of dangerous set pieces were sent over by Ryan Manning, Southampton fans were singing “we’ll score when we want”.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

But as the game passed through a flurry of substitutions Eckert’s team were unable to generate enough momentum to truly unsettle Dionisi’s men. Their only further chance came in added time and was scuffed wide by Taylor Harwood-Bellis.

Eckert said he had been happy enough with his team’s performance beyond “two errors in possession”. He insisted his squad are “very close and united” as a group. “We had a different expectation for the result but the group looks united and we now need to turn that into results.”

Opening matches rarely offer much insight into how a season will pan out. But Watford fans were able to enjoy both temperate weather and a decent performance. If Southampton want to transform the negative energy of Spygate into something positive, meanwhile, they will have to start again next week.

Sports.title: Cristiano Ronaldo says this year is ‘probably’ his last as a footballer
Sports.content:
Cristiano Ronaldo believes this year is “probably” his last as a professional footballer, the 41-year-old Portugal captain said in an interview with Vogue magazine published on Sunday.

Ronaldo, who has established his place among football’s all-time greats with more than 950 goals for club and country, had previously spoken of retiring “soon” or within “one or two years”.

“This is probably my last year of football, and I want to leave a spectacular legacy,” the Al-Nassr forward told Vogue, saying his future after football was “all mapped out”.

“I have so many things to keep me busy that to tell you just one thing is hard,” he said, listing travel and padel among his favourite activities. “Because football could leave a big hole, you have to fill your time in various ways, not just one.”

Ronaldo married his partner, Georgina Rodríguez, in an intimate ceremony in the Portuguese resort of Cascais on Tuesday. The former Manchester United, Real Madrid and Juventus player told Vogue he wanted to “continue to enjoy what I’ve earned – what we’ve earned. Because after all it’s been 25 years with a lot of sacrifice.”

After being part of the Portugal side which reached the last 16 of the World Cup this summer, Ronaldo is due to link up with Al-Nassr for the new Saudi Pro League season.

Sports.title: Leicester learn harsh reality of life in League One but youngsters provide silver lining
Sports.content:
If Leicester thought this season was going to be the footballing equivalent of a gap year, visiting new places and learning some life lessons before returning home, then they were mistaken. Being outfought and outperformed by Notts County, a well-organised and energetic team promoted from the fourth tier, brought the harsh reality of life to the fore on Saturday.

Russell Martin’s desire to play out from the back provided the fragile foundation of a dispiriting performance for a team tipped to storm back up. Ollie Cooper charging down the ponderous Alex McCarthy before seeing the ball bounce back off the crossbar welcomed Leicester to League One within six minutes. McCarthy or the confused centre-back pairing of Caleb Okoli and Harry Souttar repeatedly gave the ball away in and around the penalty area as the team created their own problems. Things went so badly that a compilation of their slapstick defending quickly gained traction on social media.

Jayden Joseph gave Leicester an undeserved lead, but it did not ignite an improvement and they inevitably gave away an equaliser through further ineptitude at the back as no one reacted quickly enough to a dangerous situation, allowing the unmarked Conor Grant to pounce in the six-yard box.

With most of the sell-out crowd of 17,172 celebrating their own uplift, and the rapid demise of their rivals, Leicester struggled to cope with the intensity. “We’ve got loads of learning to do and we’ll be better for that, much better,” Martin said.

This was the first league meeting between the clubs since 1994 because they have been on very different paths over the past 32 years. There was plenty of passion for this rare East Midlands derby with County back at this level for the first time since 2014-15 and Leicester fans making the short trip to prove devotion is not determined by trophies and success. They also showed displeasure at the ownership that has overseen the slide and earned the right to boo as their viewing journeyed between subpar and unacceptable.

“A bit of anxiety crept in, the atmosphere changed in the stadium, and that’s the biggest learning for us,” Martin said. “If we don’t look after each other with the ball, like we didn’t towards the end, then it doesn’t suit us.”

View image in fullscreen Jayden Joseph put Leicester ahead in their 1-1 draw against Notts County at Meadow Lane. Photograph: David Rogers/Getty Images

When Leicester won the Premier League a decade ago, County finished 17th in League Two and went on to spend four years in the National League. Leicester may think their reputation should mean they are playing on the other side of the River Trent at the City Ground, but that scenario is a long way off on this evidence.

The uncertainty among the Leicester defence was in tune with the club’s overall situation. A sale brochure has been created to market the club for a takeover, but Martin has not received word that Leicester are officially for sale, despite reports of the owner, King Power, wanting more than £200m. It would seem difficult to reach such a figure based on the distressed nature of the asset, despite a £100m training ground and players such as Oliver Skipp, who cost £20m. For comparison, County train at the local university and their most expensive summer signing was £200,000.

Among the misery, the silver lining is that dropping down the pyramid and selling off assets opens up opportunities for young players. Will Alves, Joseph and Sammy Braybrooke started and looked the most adept in difficult circumstances, while their more illustrious colleagues hid from battle. The trio spent last season on loan in either the third or fourth tier and that experience among those relegated from the Championship was an ideal fit. The expensive Premier League signings Okoli and Skipp were not representative of their CVs, while the forwards were blunt.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“I said to people it’s not going to be easy,” Martin said. “The first day of the season, we get some crazy results. This was not an easy fixture on Sky; early kick-off; a team that got promoted last year, just down the road. We take it and we move on. And we have to improve next week.”

It cannot be easy being in the Leicester ranks, with their best players being quickly sold after relegation to bring in funds and questions remaining over others. Stephy Mavididi and Wout Faes missed the match after receiving bids, while the captain, Souttar, has interest from Championship sides. Given the unsettled and youthful nature of the squad, some pragmatism would not go amiss, but that is not Martin’s style.

One of Leicester’s key selling points is, according to the brochure, their “140-year storied history”, but their efforts here will not even make a footnote. Leicester cannot assume previous success will mean either promotion or a quick sale. It is a club in a state of flux, lacking certainty on and off the pitch. If they hoped the trip to Meadow Lane would be the start of the uplift, they were sorely misguided.

Sports.title: Young, foreign and full of adventure... new Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli is everything his predecessor wasn't
Sports.content:
As is so often the case with managerial changes made in the aftermath of failure, Scotland appear to have turned on their heels and gone in a completely new direction with the appointment of Sebastien Pocognoli.

After the young Belgian was tonight confirmed as the national side’s next head coach, it’s clear the Scottish FA will be getting a man who could hardly be more different to his predecessor.

While Steve Clarke was experienced and pragmatic, but also dour and, well, Scottish, Pocognoli is a thrusting 39-year-old adventurer who will become only the second overseas coach in the country’s history, the first since Berti Vogts over two decades back.

Pocognoli and Clarke do have in common a passion for protecting and caring for their players, but this appointment is something entirely new for Scottish football’s governing body, who are recognising the nationwide appetite for change after this summer’s World Cup group-stage exit.

Yes, Clarke made history by taking Scotland to the finals of three major tournaments, but the Tartan Army ran out patience with his caution on the big stage and with his loyalty to players who were nearing, if not past, their sell-by date at that level.

And so, the SFA have sought to address those concerns with an imaginative appointment — Ole Gunnar Solskjaer is also reported to have been interviewed — whose profile, front-foot philosophy and touchline emotion will shake things up at Hampden Park.

New Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli will be an emotional presence on the touchline

Pocognoli's passion has prompted comparisons with Atletico Madrid manager Diego Simeone

Steve Clarke's caution on the big stage grew increasingly frustrating for the Tartan Army

Of course, it helps to tap into a fashion at times like these. Pocognoli’s biggest coaching success was at Union Saint-Gilloise, who benefited from Tony Bloom and his Jamestown Analytics empire long before Hearts. Don’t be surprised if ‘data-based’ gets a mention when Ian Maxwell and Mike Mulraney get round to explaining their rationale this week.

The season before last, Pocognoli made history by leading USG to their first league title since 1935. He also inspired them to a Belgian Cup triumph during a campaign that earned him the country’s manager of the year award. The club’s first-ever Champions League experience included victories away to PSV Eindhoven and Galatasaray.

All that earned Pocognoli a move to Monaco in October, but he lasted only seven months in the job. That was despite a 10-game unbeaten sequence and a run to the knockout playoff round of the Champions League, where they were pipped 5-4 on aggregate by Paris Saint-Germain.

He is an exciting proposition. While his coaching career is still in its infancy, he has already earned himself a reputation as a forthright, demonstrative coach, fiercely protective of his team and adept at psyching them up with stirring messages and disrespectful quotes from opponents.

Born in the Belgian city of Seraing, he is of Italian descent. Often dressed entirely in black, he is sometimes compared with the Atletico Madrid manager, Diego Simeone, although Pocognoli insists that the parallel extends no further than their personalities.

In an interview earlier this year, he said: ‘I am not calm. There is a lot of fire burning inside me — the Latin blood in my veins undoubtedly has something to do with that. My grandfathers were Italian.

‘I know about the comparison with myself and Diego Simeone. Simeone is a good coach, but he is not my great role model. Atletico Madrid’s playing style doesn’t appeal to me much either. At most, we share our Latin temperament.’

While Simeone is renowned for his teams’ counter-attacking strengths, Pocognoli takes a possession-based approach that features aggressive pressing and counter-pressing. After putting in place a structure that gives him peace of mind — 3-4-1-2 is his preferred formation — he wants players to express themselves. ‘I am very self-confident,’ he says. ‘I don’t doubt easily.’

On his arrival at Monaco from USG, Pocognoli was asked to elaborate on his principles. ‘There are two aspects: the collective and the individual,’ he replied. ‘My role is to establish a structure where the defenders are dependent on the work of the attackers. This is what my team did very well last year. This resulted in one of the best defences in Europe.’

As a player, Pocognoli performed well enough at left-back to earn 13 Belgium caps, although he never made it to a World Cup finals. He was involved when the country’s golden generation emerged, but he was also party to the regional factionalism that held it back. After a 4-2 home defeat by Bosnia-Herzegovina in 2009, he had a notorious dressing-room altercation with Timmy Simons and Stijn Stijnen, who accused him of not taking the result seriously.

Pocognoli started his playing career with Genk before joining AZ Alkmaar, where he won the Dutch title. After a move to Standard Liege and then Hannover 96, he had a three-year spell in England, notable mostly for his struggles at West Bromwich Albion. Out of favour with manager Tony Pulis, he went on to loan to Brighton before returning to his homeland.

The last days of his playing career were spent with USG, where he became coach of their Under-21s. That was followed by a spell in charge of Genk’s Under-18s and an age-group job with the Belgian national side before the big break came his way.

Even USG could not have imagined that, in his debut season as a manager in his own right, he would become the youngest in Belgium’s history to win a league title. Emboldened by that early success, he is hungry for more, inspired perhaps by some of the big names he has learned from.

Former Belgium team-mate Vincent Kompany is one of his role models. As is Louis van Gaal, the ‘most complete’ manager he has worked with. Pocognoli appreciated the Dutchman’s honesty when he played for him at AZ Alkmaar. ‘He taught me the most, tactically and technically. He had a very direct way of communicating, which shocked me a little at first.’

How Pocognoli, nicknamed ‘Poco’, adapts to international football should be fascinating. Will his limited access to players allow him to instil in them his distinctive way of playing? How will he fare without the recruitment that was crucial to his success in Belgium?

When he was a boy, Pocognoli wasn’t so keen on football and had ambitions to be an archaeologist. ‘I’ve always been interested in travel, culture, and adventure,’ he says. ‘Humanity inspires me. That’s what I love about my job: mixing cultures, learning from others.’

His next managerial experience will be an education all right. Let’s hope the cross-cultural experiment benefits Scotland as much as it does him.

Sports.title: Jack Grealish is still adored by Man City fans and staff but Community Shield cameo felt like a forlorn farewell, writes JACK GAUGHAN - and Enzo Maresca already has his wildcard option on their books
Sports.content:
Jack Grealish is still adored by Man City fans and staff but Community Shield cameo felt like a forlorn farewell, writes JACK GAUGHAN - and Enzo Maresca already has his wildcard option on their books

Unlock more from Jack Gaughan inside the Man City camp with a DailyMail+ subscription - brilliant exclusives, in-depth insight, analysis and more

The odds exceptionally lengthy, the name not on anybody’s bingo card. Maybe a quiz question in years to come, albeit a slightly tame one.

Jack Grealish was the first substitution of Enzo Maresca’s era at Manchester City, called during half time of what started as an abject afternoon and never recovered.

Grealish, the man with one Premier League start to his name for the club since December 2024, was out on the Principality pitch on his own as Maresca debriefed everybody else on a horrible first half inside.

Two members of the performance staff put him through his paces before set-piece coach James French emerged with an iPad. Presumably the message was to win some free-kicks, because City could barely lay a glove from open play.

And when Martin Odegaard poleaxed Grealish as he skipped beyond the Arsenal captain with an impish first touch, it felt like old times. But those are unlikely to return permanently. City are waiting for buyers, although one is unlikely to be Everton.

Grealish had started last season’s loan spell positively, with some even calling for an international recall after a string of assists, but his influence had waned before a stress fracture in his foot ended the campaign prematurely shortly after New Year.

A question mark looms over Jack Grealish's future - but on Sunday, he was the first substitute of the Enzo Maresca era

Man City are set to entertain buyers for the former England star but a reunion with David Moyes at Everton is off the cards

The Toffees have all but opted against going back in for the 30-year-old, shying away from a return after David Moyes had a sustained period of time working with him. There is interest from other Premier League clubs, although they are thought to have more pressing priorities in the transfer window. That indicates that an answer on his future might linger for a while yet.

‘Overall I think Jack was good,’ Maresca said. ‘The ones who are still here and want to work every day… if they deserve it, they're going to get minutes. At the moment the transfer window is open and we will see what happens.’

What Grealish’s introduction did indicate is the need for City to move in the market. Savinho – who is hopeful of pushing through a move to Tottenham - was not in Cardiff after being described as unwell when missing training in the week. With youngster Ryan McAidoo nursing a shoulder problem sustained during the pre-season tour of Asia, Maresca was without other options on the bench in that area of the pitch.

If Savinho does get his wish, the only natural, senior wingers on the books expected to have a true impact this season are Jeremy Doku and Antoine Semenyo, with City needing to sign reinforcements.

McAidoo will be given the chance to prove himself as a supplementary wildcard option, probably utilised in the cup competitions. Clearly not the immediate answer, despite undoubted talent. He has impressed the new manager with a direct style and willingness to beat a man one-on-one, something that Grealish rarely counts on. His best under Pep Guardiola came in acting as the integral ball carrier during the run to the Treble, winning fouls like the one committed by Odegaard or shielding possession, allowing City to pick their moments.

Academy youngster Ryan McAidoo will hope to prove himself to Maresca this season in cup ties

All the noises around how Maresca wants this team to play suggest that those skills are not necessarily top of the list of essentials required to flourish in this team. Grealish’s six-year contract finally expires next summer and it would be more likely that someone takes him on a temporary deal than permanent at this stage.

Grealish would have headed off on tour had he not suffered an injury, doing rehabilitation in Majorca with club staff – Real Mallorca also welcomed Elliot Anderson for a tune up – and then was back training with the squad over the past few days. England boss Thomas Tuchel visited his holiday home in the area around the same time as Grealish’s fitness camp.

City have changed their squad numbers, with Grealish wearing the No 18 these days. Rayan Cherki, the mercurial attacking midfielder who couldn’t hide his frustration at lacklustre displays from team mates in the Welsh capital, has taken the No 10.

There remains adoration for him, though. The loudest cheer of the afternoon from an understandably subdued City end came as the former Aston Villa captain trotted behind David Raya’s goal to warm up in front of them. There is still a great deal of warmth for somebody who will always go down in the pantheon, purely for his role in 2023, and a willingness for him to succeed.

That is the same at Everton, Grealish hugely popular with staff, but his career almost certainly lies away from both of those clubs now. It is down to somebody else to harness obvious talent that has not shone brightly enough for three years. It is down to him to recapture the love and dedication to the craft that remains in the locker.

It’s been missing for too long yet the way he longingly stared into the distance as Arsenal celebrated at full time did suggest that these days do mean something to him. The best result for City and Grealish is that a destination giving him both of those things is found sooner rather than later.

Sports.title: Amy Hunt makes history as 'track goddess' claims her FOURTH European Championships gold with Team GB mixed 4x100m relay triumph
Sports.content:
Amy Hunt makes history as 'track goddess' claims her FOURTH European Championships gold with Team GB mixed 4x100m relay triumph

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

With arms outstretched and a grin almost as wide, Amy Hunt signed off from these European Championships in the same way she began – by claiming a gold medal. Make that four in the space of a week and a slice of history.

No woman has ever won so many from a single sitting at this level, but a perfect week for Hunt was concluded by dragging Britain to victory via a tricky spot in the mixed 4x100m relay.

Added to a gold medal secured later in the evening by Georgia Hunter Bell, and team gold in the female marathon, it was stunning day for British women in Birmingham. But Hunt was the star. Hunt was the show. Hunt was the breakthrough act that offers rich promise for the second half of this Olympic cycle.

That much was shown again on closing night, in a new relay format that has the ring of a gimmick but leant itself to an unexpectedly tight race.

It started inauspiciously when Jeremiah Azu, the men’s silver medallist, left Dina Asher-Smith in fourth at the first change, before the former 200m world champion launched her team back into the lead with a superb leg of 10.04sec. But even then, there was work to do because Zharnel Hughes, surprisingly selected ahead of Romell Glave, lost the lead to Germany.

Enter Hunt. Taking the baton for the anchor leg, she was 0.03sec behind Gina Luckenkemper, but demolished that deficit in a handful of those long strides before seeing off the closing portion in just 9.86sec. Clocking 39.97sec, 0.14sec clear of Germany, Britain had another gold and so did Hunt.

Amy Hunt helped Team GB claim gold in the mixed 100m relay on Sunday evening

The self-styled 'track goddess' aimed for a historic four medals and won them without skipping a beat

‘Oh my gosh, I am over the moon,’ said Hunt, 24. ‘To finish it off with some of my best friends in the sport is incredible.

‘Me and Jeremiah have the same birthday, so we're kind of twins. To do it all together is incredible.’

Indicating that there had been a late change of plans to the line-up, Hunt also disclosed she had only practised handovers with Hughes an hour before the gun. Clearly they had the raw speed to cope.

While Hunt’s haul is unprecedented, it will be noted that the mixed relay was only introduced this year. But that will not be counted against a Cambridge graduate who destroyed all-comers as an individual in the 100m and 200m and has added two relay titles in the course of a single weekend. She once described herself as a ‘track goddess and academic badass’ and the counter-arguments are getting harder to stage.

The forthcoming intrigue will centre on how she competes at the World Championships next year, where the best of the United States and Caribbean might offer better perspective of her level. As for Asher-Smith, 30, this was the eighth European gold medal of her career and 11th of any shade, giving her the outright female record in the 92 years of the championship.

Less than an hour later, Hunter Bell secured gold of her own in the 1500m, with a victory that was easier to predict than any of the past week. With the exception of France’s Agathe Guillemot, no one in this field had ticked off the distance within three seconds of her best mark for 2026.

But it is one thing to stand apart on paper and another to dance through the tactical minefield of a race at the sport’s most complex distance. Hunter Bell’s approach was delightfully straightforward – she set a slow pace from the front and then kicked them all the smithereens in the final 300m when Klaudia Kazimierska attempted a challenge on the last lap. Crossing in 4:07.78, Hunt Bell was well over a second clear of the Pole in silver.

Hunt praised some of her 'best friends' in the sport - team-mates Zharnel Hughes, Jeremiah Azu, and Dina Asher-Smith

Georgia Hunter Bell blew away her competition with another faultless 1500m performance

For those who follow track and field, Hunter Bell’s story is well known by now, but fresh audiences ought to watch in awe of a woman who quit for five years in her twenties and only turned professional after Olympic bronze in 2024. Prior to that decision, she was working in cyber security; in the two years since, she has now seven international medals, including golds this season at the world indoors, Commonwealth Games and here. Remarkable.

The tone for British women was set earlier in the day, when Abbie Donnelly took bronze in the marathon – the first British female to ever step on that particular podium. Coupled with the elevated placings of Natasha Wilson (fifth) and Rose Harvey (14th), Donnelly led Britain to the team gold.

Jazmin Sawyers, competing two years after rupturing an Achilles tendon, took an impressive silver in a high-level long jump showdown. Her season best mark 6.99m was only bettered by Italy’s Larissa Iapichino.

Both the men’s and women’s 4x400m teams took silver, carrying Britain to 19 medals for the Championship, but the latter’s narrow loss to Italy gave the Italians top spot in the final table.

Sports.title: Enzo Maresca admits Man City were 'not switched on' in dismal 3-0 Community Shield defeat and calls for transfers - while Mikel Arteta predicts huge season for Martin Odegaard after starring role
Sports.content:
Enzo Maresca wants Manchester City to be active in the transfer market before their Premier League campaign starts on Sunday — after Barcelona finally agreed a £65.4million deal to sign Rodri.

City’s 3-0 defeat by Arsenal in the Community Shield laid bare the need for central midfield reinforcements, though a move for Lille and Morocco midfielder Ayyoub Bouaddi is nearing completion.

Barca are finalising an agreement to land Rodri, who was not with Maresca’s squad in Cardiff.

‘Rodri is a player who just won the World Cup and Ballon d’Or,’ said Maresca before news of the agreement broke.

‘He’s a top player, all the teams need a player like Rodri, so it’s not about if we miss Rodri or not.’

City still hold an interest in Chelsea’s Enzo Fernandez, despite the Blues’ Friday deadline to lodge a £120m bid having passed without a formal offer being made.

Enzo Maresca has called for more transfer activity after Man City's 3-0 loss to Arsenal in the Community Shield

Man City are closing on a deal for Ayyoub Bouaddi, but Barcelona are expected to make another push this week to sign £70m-rated Rodri

‘He [Bouaddi] is still a Lille player,’ Maresca said of the 18-year-old. ‘Any new signing, the sooner they arrive the better because we are starting the Premier League in one week [City begin with a trip to Brighton on Sunday].

‘If they start to work with us as soon as possible it’s better so they can understand the way we want to play.’

Bouaddi — who was on the bench as Lille drew at Everton in a pre-season friendly on Saturday — wants to join City and the French club’s boss Davide Ancelotti confirmed there had been negotiations between the clubs.

Tijjani Reijnders is joining Al Qadsiah in Saudi Arabia for £52m after just one season at the club and Maresca admitted there is business City need to do if they are to compete for the biggest trophies again this season.

Elliot Anderson, Nico O’Reilly, Jeremy Doku and Erling Haaland all started the Community Shield, despite only returning to training in midweek.

‘Elliot was quite good for his first game,’ said Maresca. ‘We decided to start with four who had just two or three sessions.

ODEGAARD STEALS THE SHOW Mikel Arteta said Arsenal can use their Community Shield thrashing of Manchester City to lay down a marker to their rivals ahead of the club's Premier League title defence. The Gunners eased past Enzo Maresca’s men after first-half goals from Riccardo Calafiori and Kai Havertz, before Martin Odegaard added the gloss on 48 minutes in a ruthless display. The north London club’s victory over the FA Cup holders gave them their second trophy in four months and their 18th Community Shield title overall, leaving Arteta purring. '(I'm) very impressed in the manner that we played, especially in the manner that we competed so that's a standard for us and if we have the standards at this level I'm sure that we're going to be really competitive,' warned Arteta. 'Probably there's more belief (after winning title), you know how to do it, you know what it takes to win it and the contribution of everybody because last season that was the biggest asset of the team. Every single player contributed to make us champions and we know that that's going to be exactly the same. ‘I'm obviously extremely happy with the performance, the results and winning the first trophy. We talked about the desire that we have to start the season and to show ourselves how much we want it, and I certainly saw a lot of positive things there against a top opponent.’ Odegaard stole the show as he led from the front after an injury-plagued last season. Arteta believes a different Odegaard will be raring to prove a point this time around. He added: ‘Well, he (Odegaard) missed five or six months for different things and it was extremely difficult for him to get any momentum, so I'm sure this year if we can maintain him fit, available with the players around him, we're going to see a very different Martin. ‘And I sense from the first day that he joined that he has something else in the belly that he wants to prove and show it, because the team needs it as well.’ ISAAN KHAN

‘The reason was because sometimes players prefer to start. The plan was to change all of them after 45 minutes, or an hour maximum.’

City started sluggishly, conceding inside the first minute, and Maresca criticised his team for not being ‘switched on’.

Captain Ruben Dias said the display was ‘frustrating’. He added: ‘It’s not good enough. Many things are changing, a new manager as well. If there is a lesson to be learned in a final, let it be this one because there are a lot more coming.

‘The most important thing is we’re already looking forward and we’ll be ready for our next game.’

Sports.title: Pre-season fight club: How Premier League 'friendlies' became anything but, with red cards, brutal challenges and even a heated row between team-mates
Sports.content:
Pre-season fight club: How Premier League 'friendlies' became anything but, with red cards, brutal challenges and even a heated row between team-mates

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

As Premier League teams prepare for the fast-approaching 2026-27 season, they've been trudging their way through their customary pre-season friendlies.

This year, however, many of these matches have been anything but friendly, featuring a litany of questionable challenges, red cards and mass confrontations.

Daily Mail Sport takes a look at those in question....

A Spurs scuffle

Sandro Tonali wasted no time demonstrating his competitive spirit in a Spurs shirt during their behind-closed-doors match against Spanish side Getafe.

The Italian, signed in a blockbuster £100m deal from Newcastle this summer, reacted furiously following a late challenge by Getafe's defensive midfielder Mario Martin. Tonali responded to his counterpart's short-sighted attempt at playing the ball by menacingly stalking him up the pitch before landing a few ill-tempered jabs to his chest.

A small scuffle ensued which was quickly broken up by Tottenham stalwart Ben Davies and Tonali's fellow new signings Andrew Robertson and Jan Paul van Hecke.

🎥 Sandro Tonali scuffle in pre-season 🇮🇹 pic.twitter.com/XTGblesDyj — The Spurs Watch (@TheSpursWatch) August 8, 2026

Tonali was left incensed by a challenge from Getafe's Mario Martin, rushing up behind him and shoving him several times, including once to the neck

Several Getafe players rushed towards Tonali and the approaching referee after the incident

Elanga brutally chopped down

Anthony Elanga's pre-season preparations were cut brutally short when the winger was carried off on a stretcher following a terrible challenge from Valencia captain Jose Gaya.

The Spaniard was immediately sent off following the challenge, which sparked a mass confrontation between both sets of players. Elanga was left visibly distressed as he was carried off the pitch, though new boss Matthias Jaissle later provided some relief by confirming that his injury is not quite as serious as first thought.

Following a year in which the majority of the Magpies' star players have been poached, many Newcastle fans are looking to the likes of Elanga to step up as they seek to improve on a dismal 12th place finish last season.

Penalty chaos

Chelsea's Far East tour descended into chaos in Malaysia after striker Liam Delap fell victim to a horror challenge at the behest of Johor Darul Ta'zim defender Antonio Cristian.

In a game with no shortage of shirt pulling, nasty challenges and heated arguments, it was the Spanish defender's reckless attempt to play the ball through his man that saw it reach a boiling point.

Following the full-time whistle, Johor Darul Ta'zim players refused to participate in the penalty shootout that has become customary at the end of many pre-season matches this summer, resulting in a confusing end to a game which featured six goals and seven yellow cards.

Even Chelsea's set-piece coach Austin MacPhee appeared to want a piece of the action, pictured getting into a heated confrontation with a member of the Johor Darul Ta'zim bench as they headed down the tunnel.

A rare friendly red

Bournemouth star Alex Scott and former Manchester United man Antony were both sent off during the Premier League side's clash with Real Betis in southern Spain.

The incident, which began when Colombian midfielder Nelson Deossa rifled the ball at Bournemouth's Bafode Diakite, saw players from both sides embroiled in a fierce confrontation. The confrontation quickly escalated before Scott and Antony were dismissed for aggressively shoving one another. Truthfully, the actions of the two players, who both arrived late to the brawl, were no more egregious than those of their team-mates.

Cherries fans will, however, be thankful that preseason red cards do not constitute a ban in competitive matches and the attacking midfielder will be available to play in Bournemouth's opening Premier League fixture against Manchester City.

‘Tangana’ en el Real Betis-Bournemouth que acaba con las expulsiones directas de Antony y Scott.



Surrealista. pic.twitter.com/yAsIWOzdAP — Gonzalo Tortosa (@GonzaloTortosa) August 8, 2026

Bournemouth's Alex Scott and Real Betis' Antony were sent off after a clash during their pre-season friendly

Former Man United winger Antony caused a confrontation between the two teams on the stroke of half-time

Scott was shown a red card for his involvement after he was seen pushing Antony away

Angry Arbeloa

It was new manager Alvaro Arbeloa who saw red in Fulham's penultimate pre-season match on Wednesday.

Following the awarding of a contentious 89th-minute penalty for the hosts, Arbeloa was pictured shaking his head in disbelief on the bench, a stark contrast to the incredulous smiles sported by his players. The Spaniard stormed onto the pitch following the full-time whistle, furiously protested the referee's decision and was promptly dismissed. The Fulham players followed their manager into the dressing room, refusing to take part in the expected penalty shootout and forfeiting the match.

Arriving after a turbulent stint at Real Madrid last season, the Spaniard has seemingly arrived in west London with a point to prove, with many questioning if such an inexperienced manager is the right choice following the high-profile departures of Harry Wilson and Raul Jimenez.

Fulham manager Alvaro Arbeloa was sent off after full-time of their 2-2 draw at Malaga

Row between team-mates

Liverpool's stateside pre-season clash with Wrexham devolved into a domestic as several senior players clashed over who should've been given the captain's armband following stand-in skipper Dominik Szoboszlai's substitution.

In the moments immediately following the full-time whistle, Curtis Jones, who is wanted by Inter Milan, ran up to confront Szoboslai about his decision to hand the armband to Kostas Tsimikas. Tensions flared between the trio, culminating in the Greek full-back throwing the armband to the ground in dramatic fashion.

With Liverpool looking to recover from a disappointing season under Arne Slot, and in the wake of seasoned veterans Mohamed Salah and Robertson's departures, it appears the Reds may have a leadership crisis on their hands.

Sports.title: Jamie Vardy mulls surprise move to Brazil after receiving a 'considerable' offer from Sao Paulo - with West Ham also in talks with striker
Sports.content:
Jamie Vardy mulls surprise move to Brazil after receiving a 'considerable' offer from Sao Paulo - with West Ham also in talks with striker

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Jamie Vardy has held talks with Brazilian side Sao Paulo.

Negotiations are in the early stages but it is understood to be a considerable offer from one of Brazil's biggest clubs who have just come out of a transfer embargo.

The 39-year-old is considering the ambitious move despite initially planning a fairytale return to the Premier League.

The former England striker has also spoken to West Ham among others.

The ex-Leicester forward wants to take his time to make the right decision for his family as they felt they rushed into their move to Cremonese last year despite valuing the experience.

Vardy had an option to stay for another season with the Lombardy outfit had they remained in Serie A.

Jamie Vardy is considering a surprise move to Brazil after receiving an early stage offer

As a free agent he can join clubs outside of the transfer window but ideally wants to decide before then.

Vardy called time on his 13-season stint at the Foxes at the end of the 2024-25 season as the club's greatest-ever player.

The former non-league star scored his 200th goal for Leicester in the dying stages of that campaign, after announcing his departure in April of last year.

The striker was instrumental to the club's golden spell in the 2010s, winning the Premier League, the FA Cup, and the Championship twice.

Sports.title: New Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli vows to build a team the Tartan Army can be proud of
Sports.content:
New Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli vows to build a team the Tartan Army can be proud of

Sebastien Pocognoli has been confirmed as the new Scotland head coach after signing an initial two-year contract to succeed Steve Clarke.

The former Union Saint-Gilloise and Monaco head coach becomes Scotland’s second foreign manager following German Berti Vogts’ reign from 2002-04.

Pocognoli, a former Belgium international, led Union to the 2024-25 Belgian title in his first season as a head coach.

The 39-year-old described his appointment as an ‘honour’ and added on the Scottish Football Association website: ‘When I first heard of the interest, I was immediately excited about the opportunity.

‘Scotland’s supporters are famous for their passion — most recently at the World Cup in the USA — and I have experienced it myself as a player for Belgium when we played in 2013.

‘Along with my coaching staff, I will do everything I can to give them a team to be proud of and build on the success that has been achieved already by my predecessor.’

Sebastien Pocognoli has been confirmed as the new manager of Scotland's national team

The former West Brom and Brighton left-back will aim to build on Clarke’s record of leading Scotland to their first three major tournaments of the century.

‘Since negotiations began, I have been doing a lot of research, asking a lot of questions and looking at areas that we can build on,’ he said. ‘I am hugely excited by the prospect and look forward to working with the players to achieve even more success.’

After leading Union to their first ever title success, Pocognoli joined Monaco in October last year. He took them into the Champions League knockout phase, where they lost narrowly to Paris St Germain, but was sacked after a seventh-placed finish in Ligue 1.

SFA chief executive Ian Maxwell said: ‘He was the standout candidate from a thorough process: a very impressive individual, with a real desire to take on the role and a clear vision for how he wants to go about it.’

The SFA’s recently appointed chief football officer Craig Mulholland was heavily involved in the process amid sweeping changes to the national team set-up which have also seen the departure of Under-21 coach Scot Gemmill and Under-17s coach Brian McLaughlin.

Pocognoli was previously manager of Union Saint-Gilloise and, most recently, Monaco

Mulholland described the appointment as an ‘exciting moment for Scottish football’ and added: ‘He is one of Europe’s brightest and most sought-after coaches.

‘He will bring an aggressive, front-foot style of play that will excite supporters. He will now build on the outstanding work and excellent foundations left by Steve Clarke and his staff.

‘While our extensive search was informed by data and insight — and Sebastien’s metrics matched what we believe necessary to enhance and evolve from a position of strength — it’s as important to us that his personality and character will allow him to connect with a fantastic group of players.’

Pocognoli will begin his tenure with a Nations League campaign against Slovenia, North Macedonia and Switzerland with his first game in charge coming in Ljubljana on September 26.

Sports.title: Juventus reopen talks with Tottenham's Guglielmo Vicario after Emiliano Martinez deal collapses, and Al Hilal target Chelsea's Pedro Neto: WINDOW WATCH
Sports.content:
It's that time of the year again – the transfer window is now open until September 1 and it's sure to be a busy period as clubs look to make big signings ahead of the new season.

Here are today's latest developments from Simon Jones and the Daily Mail Sport team...

Juve back in for Spurs' Vicario

Juventus have resumed contacts for Tottenham goalkeeper Guglielmo Vicario after talks for Aston Villa's Emiliano Martinez collapsed on Sunday night.

The Serie A club made an initial offer of £6million, plus performance-related bonuses for Martinez and his advisors agreed terms with Juventus intermediaries on a significant rise on his current £130,000 a week.

However, despite initial optimism, Juventus have pulled back from the deal and are back in talks for 29-year-old Vicario.

Villa have agreed a £30m deal with Parma for goalkeeper Zion Suzuki, who will sign a five-year contract. The Japan international is expected to become their new number one so a solution will be required for Martinez.

Tottenham goalkeeper Guglielmo Vicario is again the subject of interest from Juventus after the club's move for Emiliano Martinez collapsedc

Bolton's McAtee targeted by four clubs

Bolton Wanderers forward John McAtee is attracting interest from a number of Championship clubs, with Charlton Athletic, Cardiff City, Lincoln City as well as Sheffield Wednesday all understood to have made enquiries regarding the 27-year-old.

McAtee produced an impressive performance on the club's return to the Championship on Saturday, registering two assists as Bolton secured a memorable 2-1 victory over Preston North End in their first game back in the second tier for seven years.

The Salford born forward, who turned 27 last month, has built a reputation as a versatile and hard-working attacking player capable of operating across the front line. He joined Bolton in 2024 and has made a significant contribution since arriving at the club.

His performance against Preston is likely to further increase interest, with a number of clubs now monitoring his situation as the transfer window enters its final few weeks.

McAtee, who turned 27 last month, has built a reputation as a versatile and hard-working attacking player capable of operating across the front line

Stoke's Seko heads home

Japanese midfielder Tatsuki Seko has left Stoke City to join J1 League side Urawa Reds for an undisclosed fee.

The 28-year-old returns to Japan after two seasons in the Championship with the Potters, having arrived from Kawasaki Frontale in the summer of 2024.

Newcastle keep Bergvall in their sights

Lucas Bergvall is one of the names that remains on Newcastle United's radar in the final days of the window.

While talks have taken place for Bayern Munich’s Joao Palhinha, other midfielders are being considered.

Newcastle discussed Bergvall as part of conversations over the sale of Sandro Tonali to Tottenham.

Newcastle made further enquiries after Tonali’s sale but were told the fee would be over £50m for Bergvall.

Nottingham Forest are also expected to make another offer for the Swede.

Newcastle discussed Bergvall as part of conversations over the sale of Tonali to Tottenham and made further enquiries after but were told the fee would be over £50m

Hammers turn attention to Piroe

West Ham have enquired after Leeds United striker Joel Piroe after hitting an impasse in talks for Troy Parrott at AZ Alkmaar.

The Hammers had an opening bid around £15m rejected for Parrott last week and remained in talks offering slightly more. They could yet make another offer but as it stands the deal is paused and they have enquired about Piroe with Leeds prepared to sell.

Dedic due on Tyneside tomorrow

Benfica right-back Amar Dedic is due on Tyneside tomorrow to undergo a medical ahead of his move to Newcastle.

Negotiations are at the final stages with a £29.5million deal in place for the 23-year-old.

The Bosnia international is likely to go straight into the team to play Liverpool next weekend.

Newcastle have also held talks with Bayern Munich over a move for Joao Palhinha but have other targets they are considering.

Coventry hold talks over £21m move for striker

As reported by Daily Mail Sport last night, Coventry City are in talks with Fenebahce over a £21million deal for striker Sidiki Cherif.

As well as agreeing to sign Nottingham Forest's Taiwo Awoniyi, manager Frank Lampard wants Cherif who was a target for Crystal Palace and Wrexham in January.

The 19-year-old scored three goals in 14 games for Fenerbahce.

Neto a shock target for Al Hilal

Chelsea winger Pedro Neto is wanted by Saudi Pro League side Al Hilal.

Neto is also on the lists of Tottenham and Manchester City but Chelsea's asking price is understood to be prohibitive.

Pedro Neto has emerged as a target for Saudi Arabian club Al Hilal

Tigers in for Betis star Garcia

Hull City are in talks for Real Betis winger Pablo Garcia.

The 20-year-old is valued around £7million by Betis. He made his debut for Spain U21s a year ago and has scored three goals in five games for his country at that level.

Hull have been looking for a winger after a proposed deal for Aston Villa's Leon Bailey stalled.

Garcia has become a key player for coach Manuel Pellegrini owing to his pace and goal contributions.

He came on as a substitute for Antony last night in their 1-0 friendly defeat at Inter Milan on Sunday. John Stones scored the only goal, coming off the bench to score on his debut.

And the best of the rest...

LEEDS have agreed a deal with HAMBURG to send Sebastiaan Bornauw on loan to the German club.

FULHAM have had a £17m bid rejected for ATALANTA right-back Raoul Bellanova. The Italians are reluctant to sell the 26-year-old this summer.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"
